title: Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it
snippet: All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core. After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take. more…
fullText:
All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core.

After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take.

System

Googlebook OS looks like ChromeOS on the surface but feels like Android. However, it is more optimized than any large-screen iteration of Android to date, including foldables and especially tablets. This is infinitely better than other desktop Android experiences, especially plugging your Pixel into an external display.

There is a level of nativeness here that I always thought was missing from Chromebooks. ChromeOS from the very start felt like an extension of the web and never outgrew that in my opinion. Googlebook OS does not have that issue.

	

As a Pixel user, I quickly adjusted to the Googlebook UI and UX, with the only real learning curve being keyboard shortcuts. I think that will be true for any proficient user of Android smartphones, and that immediate familiarity could be very appealing for both the average and more advanced users.

In the top-right corner, you’ll find familiar Android status icons. A tap opens Quick Settings that are identical to the Pixel experience save for a volume slider. The bell icon opens notifications with access to notification history in the bottom-left corner.

A shortcut that activates Magic Pointer is next, useful if you don’t want to enable the “cursor wiggle” gesture. There’s also a Live Update for any currently playing media. This tiny pill shows the responsible app and track name. Hovering over the icon lets you quickly play/pause and a tap brings up full media controls, which are also available in the notification shade. On other desktop OSes, pausing media always requires two clicks, with Googlebook’s implementation a really nice touch that takes advantage of having a cursor.

The top-left corner is home to time, day, and date, with a tap opening a useful calendar, like on ChromeOS.

On the HP Googlebook 14, the F1 key is Android’s back button and a genuinely useful hardware shortcut for quickly navigating apps. F2 is a Home button that takes you to the desktop, while F3 is Recents. F4 full-screens windows and F5 is for partial screen captures. F6 and F7 let you adjust screen brightness, while F8 lets you control the keyboard backlight. F9 is a microphone mute switch that works in conjunction with the Quick Settings Tile. F10, F11, and F12 are for volume, with F13 physically letting you start voice typing with Rambler. The icons could use some revamping, especially the fullscreen and screenshot symbols as both are too similar to the Recents key and too vague for glanceability. These rely on prior knowledge and are not designed intuitively.

The Quick Insert key that’s physically shared with Caps Lock opens a floating window that lets you quickly add emoji, access copied text, recent screenshots, and tabs. Carried over from Chromebook Plus, it’s deeply integrated with Gboard from Emoji Kitchen to GIFs and Stickers. You can also access the Gboard Clipboard Manager found on phones (and leave it open as a floating window), as well as invoke voice transcription. It’s pretty useful for surfacing common functionality for those who don’t remember or expertly use keyboard shortcuts, and more than worthy of being a physical key. The capability I’m missing from my Mac workflow is a text expander for macros.

The stylized ‘G’ or Action key opens the floating app launcher. This is basically Pixel Launcher device and web search, and I wish there was Gemini integration here. You will use this key in combination with a host of other shortcuts.

The Settings app is identical to the Pixel experience, with a dual-column layout. Controls you’d expect on a desktop OS appear first with “Device & accessories.” This lets you adjust the Touchpad, Keyboard, Display, Sound, and Glowbar. You can remap Modifier keys like Caps lock, Ctrl, Action (G), and Alt.

I greatly enjoy having Android widgets on my desktop (officially the “Home screen”). The first few times I saw them on this bigger screen, I had to do a double-take. It’s amusing to see the widgets, with Dynamic Color on full display, you see all the time on your phone, but now on your desktop. The larger size makes it a great surface for passive information throughout the day. For example, I use the Google Health widget to remind me to move and quickly log water consumption. You can also place app icons and folders, as well as folders and files for quick access.

Corner shortcuts (like on Mac) are great, and let you move your cursor to any of the four corners to trigger shortcuts like “Peek/unpeek desktop” or show notifications. My favorite is a Note-taking hot corner that opens my current Google Keep note. There’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut for that.

Multi-touch and text selection are all solid and feel like a desktop OS. Touchpad gestures include swiping three fingers up to get a zoomed-out Recents view of all open windows. Meanwhile, my external keyboard works normally on Googlebooks.

That said, there are some very annoying interfaces that come directly from smartphones and just enlarged for desktops. Taking fullscreen screenshots (G + S) results in a fullscreen flash that is okay on phones but incredibly distracting on a big laptop screen. I also find the copied text pop-up, which matches mobile Android, in the bottom-right corner to be equally distracting and would like an option to disable it. Similarly, the Tap & click sounds enabled by default are very annoying.

I haven’t really found myself using Cross-device services. Notification sync that shows all your phone alerts is a straightforward capability, but I always have my phone with me when I’m working on the laptop.

I used Cast My Apps, which has a prominent access point in the Taskbar, primarily for Google Messages over the PWA (more on that later). Otherwise, I would just install any Android apps I needed directly on the Googlebook. “Continue on” is something I haven’t really used, with Google intending the feature to pick up an activity from my phone on the bigger screen.

After first setting up the device, it might take some time for these Cross-device features to become available. That in itself is a bad first impression, but worse is how Googlebooks launched without day one support for the biggest player: Samsung.

Finally, I want to genuinely applaud Google for controlling the update process, like it did with Chromebooks before, rather than allowing OEMs to do so. Manufacturer customization is limited to preloaded OEM apps, like Acer’s that provides product registration, warranty information, and system stats. 

Chrome

Under-the-hood, Chrome on Googlebooks is built upon the Android version. Functionality added to the mobile browser includes extensions support, vertical tabs, and the full Gemini in Chrome side panel.

The browser delivers desktop-class performance that has not caused any website compatibility issues for me this past week.

However, the page reloads you’re familiar with on phones are definitely on our 16GB Googlebooks. There are also annoyances like Chrome Settings opening as a fullscreen interface that replaces all your other browser windows. Another is how right-click desktop menu items you expect are not available. Opening a new window (including Incognito) also won’t let you type until you tap the URL bar, unlike Chrome on every other desktop platform. For this initial release, Google did not port over all functionality and the result is an experience that feels barebones.

The browser is fine for 1.0, but I very much want Google to bring over all desktop functionality and every behavior — no matter how small — to this version. Chrome is truly a constant in most people’s desktop computing history and there is so much muscle memory built over years of use that any regression feels painful.

AI

Magic Pointer is fine and basically the Gemini overlay on phones. The cursor “wiggle” gesture is fundamentally intuitive, while the persistent shortcut in the top right lets you start it without the shake. I would not mind the ability to disable the corner icon from a visual standpoint.

That said, in what feels like a prime example of shipping your org chart, both Magic Pointer and Circle to Search are available on Googlebooks. The latter, invoked by G + A, is billed as Contextual Search and arguably convenient for OCR copying, while Magic Pointer is more for taking action on information. However, it feels wild for there to be two similar features in the OS.

On Googlebook, Gemini is powered by the Google (Search) app, with the large-screen interface looking quite nice. My preferred way of accessing it is via the actual Gemini overlay, launched using G + Space bar.

The obvious and more useful AI feature is Rambler. I’ve never really used voice dictation on a desktop until Googlebook OS. It’s surprisingly hard to remember that it’s available given the full hardware keyboard in front of you, but the F13 key that starts voice input helps.

The less apparent feature is Create My Widget. Generative UI where you specify what information you want to see is the future of computing. Google is starting with a friendly widget creator that gets the point across. I’ve been using this to keep track of how the Dodgers and Yankees are progressing through the playoffs, while a flight countdown is another widget of mine. 

Apps

From life to work, I can get everything I need done in a web browser. My MacBook Air is a glorified Chromebook in that regard. 

I’ve resized most of the native Android apps I frequently use to a phone-sized window. It makes for an even more familiar experience and lets me fit more onto each screen. That said, most of Google’s large-screen layouts are pretty good at this point. 

All the Google Workspace “apps” installed on Googlebooks are Trusted Web Activities (TWAs). These are essentially Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), but support homescreen widgets. For example, Google Calendar opens calendar.google.com in a window, but you can add the schedule widget you’re familiar with from your phone.

I think Googlebooks would have been an excellent opportunity to mandate that Gmail for Android and other Workspace apps have full feature parity with their web versions, but Google’s strategy of letting developers choose whether to use the web or Android is the right call to boost adoption and support. I have not felt the need to change any of the Workspace TWAs to the Android version.

Google Keep and Tasks use their Android versions, which are better than keep.google.com and tasks.google.com, respectively. I wrote most of this review on Keep for Android.

When I reviewed the Pixel Tablet in 2023, one of my complaints was that its Google Messages app was essentially just messages.google.com/web. That has frustratingly not changed on Googlebooks. Google desperately needs to offer a native experience that would ideally just be the large-screen interface found on foldables with a sync system. 

Other Android apps I’ve been using include Pixel Weather, Recorder, and Journal (marking the first time I’ve journaled with a full-size keyboard). As a Pixel user, I’m immensely glad that these three experiences are available on Googlebooks. 

On the media front, YouTube and YouTube Music both open their websites rather than the Android apps. I’m enjoying Apple Music’s in-beta Liquid Glass redesign for the tablet interface. It’s basically the iPad app with top tabs and a floating Now Playing bar.

A big annoyance I immediately noticed in Android apps is that the primary text field is often not active and requires a tap/click. This is so annoying that I’ve found myself tapping the touchscreen rather than using the trackpad. It’s almost second nature. The issue is particularly pronounced in the Gemini app, though a new Chrome tab always selects the address bar.

In terms of native apps:

The Files app is carried over from ChromeOS with a nice, modern icon. AI file summaries that are generated locally are pretty convenient when quickly browsing.

The Text app is code-oriented with a modern Material 3 Expressive design.

The Viewer app is basic compared to macOS Preview.

The “My Googlebook” app is strangely responsible for an “Up next” widget that shows data from Google Calendar, Drive, and Keep.

Of course, there’s also the elephant in the room. For the most part, Googlebooks haven’t fixed the app gap that Chromebooks have faced for over a decade. While there have been some expansions and Android as a whole delivers more of a foundation for desktop-class apps than ChromeOS did, Google hasn’t made the partnerships or the push to actually fix the problem. Those who, like me, can already do most things from a browser will be happy, but demanding that users adopt a new platform in 2026 without staples of the desktop ecosystem — Adobe’s suite sticks out like a sore thumb — is a tough ask.

Hardware 

I’ve been using Googlebook OS full-time this past week across the Acer Googlebook 14 and HP Googlebook 14.

On the lid, the primary branding is the manufacturer’s logo followed by the Glowbar. Once open, there’s a logo beneath the screen and “Googlebook” on the left palm rest. 

The Glowbar is additive, with the battery indicator proving useful when plugging in to charge. However, I would have liked a double-tap/knock gesture to invoke it at any time to see the charge level. In public, having a strip of light facing the world feels somewhat loud. Fortunately, you can turn it off in Settings.

Face unlock has worked as expected on the HP Googlebook 14. The setup experience is identical to what’s found on Pixel phones, and I wonder if the exact same recognition algorithms are leveraged. 

This could be an edge case tied to how I use “Tap to click,” but the trackpad might be too wide on the HP as I keep unintentionally activating it with the sides of my thumbs when typing. Most times the cursor just briefly appears and then disappears. However, there are occasions when moving a hand to reach the number row registers a tap and very disruptively moves my position on the page. Disabling the option, and thus getting the benefit of the haptic trackpad, negates the latter annoyance.

For being a 2-in-1, the Acer Googlebook 14 is incredibly light with a fairly solid build. USI stylus support is nice, especially on such a large canvas.

Between Acer’s Intel chip and Snapdragon on the HP, I have to give the clear advantage to ARM. I’d say the latter runs a bit smoother, while I’ve seen fewer webpage reloads as well when over a dozen tabs/windows and several Android apps are open. 

We’ll be reviewing all five Googlebooks in the coming weeks, so stay tuned to 9to5Google.

Conclusion

	

In going all-in on Googlebook OS for the past eight days, it’s clear that Google put the work in to design a native desktop experience for Android. My biggest fear in the lead-up to using Googlebooks was that the company just stretched out Android as seen on the Pixel Tablet and the Android (16+) desktop mode. That is not the case, with a number of well-thought-out power user features and customizations.

The switch from Chromebooks to Googlebooks gives Google a solid foundation to grow. But, at the same time, it’s hard to ignore that Googlebook OS on day one has taken some clear steps back from ChromeOS. A handful of issues are expected in a strategy reset like this, but missing features (e.g., Linux app support) and other shortcomings are hard to accept when this is Google’s replacement for an OS that’s been around for over a decade now. There are no fatal flaws for the general user, but there are plenty of “death by a thousand cuts” examples that will keep even Chromebook switchers away from Googlebooks for the time being. That said, I don’t think Googlebook OS has any foundational issues that can’t be remedied in future updates.

I think I’m fairly representative of the average user in that everything I use has web-based equivalents. As such, I can use Googlebook OS for everything I do on macOS. However, the Mac has a level of system polish that I appreciate and some native applications that upgrade the workflows I have. This is my barrier to switching. 

That polish and charm are not fully there yet on Googlebook OS, but there are a number of good UI and UX ideas here. The familiarity offered by sharing the Android OS and apps from your phone is a real competitive advantage. If you know how to use an Android phone, the jump to a Googlebook will be immediate. Personally, that similarity is motivating me to add a Googlebook to my daily driver lineup. Google just needs to continue iterating and updating quickly.

title: Smartphone Shipments Just Hit a New Low. Thanks, RAMageddon
snippet: Higher phone prices are seriously squeezing consumers’ wallets, says Counterpoint Research.
fullText:
If you’re holding on to your phone despite a wave of new, high-powered options, you’re not alone. Hitting the lowest mark since 2012, smartphone shipments worldwide continued a months-long skid, slumping 20% in the third quarter of 2026 due to the RAMageddon memory shortage, according to a new analysis by Counterpoint Research.

Counterpoint said that the cost of DRAM and NAND — the two main memory chips used in smartphones, computers and data centers — continues to rise, forcing manufacturers to raise phone prices, which are up 20% overall this year. Memory costs more because there’s less of it to go around, thanks to the massive AI infrastructure buildup and its voracious appetite for chips.

It was the second consecutive quarter to take “the full brunt of the memory crisis,” Shilpi Jain, a senior analyst at Counterpoint, said in a statement Monday.

			

More from CNET

Research firm Gartner has estimated that companies will spend $1.4 trillion on AI infrastructure this year and $2.6 trillion overall. More than 70% of global memory chip production will go toward AI investment, TrendForce said. Global fears about rising inflation for most products and services are also likely suppressing phone sales.

Some manufacturers fared all right during the third quarter, according to Counterpoint. Samsung’s market share was 23%, up from 19% in 2025, thanks in part to “robust initial demand” for the Galaxy Fold 8. Apple’s third-quarter market share was 22%, the first time the company has surpassed 20% in that three-month period. But both companies saw a year-over-year decline in shipments.

Things aren’t looking rosy for customers’ wallets, either. Earlier this month, Samsung hiked prices by $100 for its Galaxy S26 phones, and Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched last month with prices set $100 above the previous generation.

How are consumers responding?

The third quarter saw a number of notable smartphone introductions, including Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, the Google Pixel 11 and, in the period’s waning days, the iPhone 18 Pro line and Apple’s first foldable, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. Preorders for the iPhone Duo begin on Friday.

Shoppers will be cautious about buying the latest and greatest in smartphones because of higher prices, says TMT analyst Paolo Pescatore.

“New design features, including foldables, may generate excitement and appeal, but their steep price premiums remain hard to justify when most people want a device that delivers robust, reliable connectivity,” Pescatore told CNET via email. “For many, the question is straightforward: why replace a perfectly functioning smartphone that continues to meet their everyday needs?”

Counterpoint Research found in a recent survey that half of respondents — spanning the US, UK, India, China and Germany — would wait until holiday sales to buy a new phone. That number rises to 56% among Gen Z consumers. Counterpoint’s Jain said consumers are increasingly shopping for “refurbished devices and prioritizing higher-value devices.”

With sales down, phonemakers might resort to different strategies for customers, including refurbished handsets, repairs and trade-in schemes, Pescatore said. Cellphone carriers like T-Mobile, Verizon Wireless and AT&T could also use financing plans and bundled services as enticements.

As AI investment continues to devour memory supply, phone prices won’t be falling anytime soon. And with companies focusing more on premium devices, there could be fewer budget alternatives available for customers, Counterpoint Research said.

title: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
snippet: Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
fullText:
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.

Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.

According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.

Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”

To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.

“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.

The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year. Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.

According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio, which came online earlier this year.

title: Chromecast with Google TV gets first update of 2026
snippet: Following the last release 11 months ago, Google is rolling out the first update of 2026 to the Chromecast with Google TV (4K). more…
fullText:
Following the last release 11 months ago, Google is rolling out the first update of 2026 to the Chromecast with Google TV (4K).

	

According to Google’s release notes, UTTA.260813.002 is rolling out just for the 4K model. There is no new release for the HD variant today. Both streaming devices are usually updated at the same time.

This update bumps the Android Security Patch Level to August 2026 (from October 2025). Google also notes the presence of “Other bug fixes and performance improvements.”

On your Chromecast with Google TV, go to Settings > System > About > System update to download and install.

title: Bumble agrees to a $1.3B acquisition deal as online dating faces a reset
snippet: After years of declining subscriber numbers and falling revenue, Bumble just agreed to a $1.3 billion acquisition.
fullText:
Bumble is getting a new owner. The dating app announced Tuesday that it has agreed to a $1.3 billion acquisition deal with Ithaca Holdings, marking a major shift for a company that once looked like one of the biggest success stories in online dating. 

The deal would take the company private after years of declining subscriber numbers, falling revenue, and mounting pressure to rethink the online dating experience. The move may give Bumble a chance to work on its next chapter away from the pressure of public markets.

Founded in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble made a name for itself for its unique approach where only women made the first move. That helped it stand out in a crowded dating market, and the company eventually went public in 2021 at a valuation of roughly $14 billion.

Since then, however, the dating app landscape has changed considerably. Bumble has faced declining paying users, weaker revenue, and growing dissatisfaction with the familiar swipe-based model. The company recently reported second-quarter 2026 revenue of $211 million, down 15.2% year over year, while its paying user base fell 16.4% to approximately 3.2 million.

The acquisition follows a review of strategic options by an independent committee of Bumble’s board, which recommended the transaction after consulting outside legal and financial advisers. Wolfe Herd did not participate in the board’s discussions or vote on the deal, according to the press release. 

“In Ithaca, we have found a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future,” Wolfe Herd said in a statement.

She also confirmed that she plans to stay actively involved in the business, working alongside Ithaca’s Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, and the Bumble team.

Going private might give Bumble more flexibility to experiment with new features and make changes without having to answer to public-market investors every quarter. The company has been exploring AI-driven features and putting more energy into helping people connect offline, reflecting a broader shift in how younger users approach dating.

One example is Plans, announced in July, which focuses on bringing people together through real-world activities. Wolfe Herd also recently revealed that the company is developing a new way for users to interact that could eventually replace the swipe-based model.

title: Honeyjar offers AI tools to improve PR and comms at every company
snippet: Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken. But could AI actually make things better?
fullText:
Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken (buy me a drink sometime, and I’ll give you my rant). But could AI actually make things better?

Honeyjar, which will be attending this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt as part of the Startup Battlefield 200, wants to use AI to make the expertise and judgment of the best PR pros available to everyone, including founders who have no idea where to start.

The startup’s founders, CEO Michelle Masek and CCO Nadia Jamshidi, certainly fit the bill when it comes to PR expertise. They’ve both spent decades in the field, doing in-house communications and working at agencies. Masek recently served as senior vice president of marketing and communications for Ev Williams’ venture firm, Obvious Ventures.

As Masek described the challenges involved in “helping with the why and when of comms and marketing for 110 portfolio companies” (the startups her firm had invested in), I flashed back to my own brief stint leading marketing at an early-stage VC firm, where founders were constantly asking for help getting into TechCrunch. So I wasn’t surprised that Masek found herself asking, “Is there a way to scale the senior-level expertise into AI [in a way] that actually helps users do the work of comms in the proactive and skilled way that we do?”

Honeyjar is her answer to that question. It automates processes like writing announcements, finding the best journalists to pitch, and identifying the most promising speaking opportunities. But Jamshidi told me in a follow-up email that Honeyjar’s vision goes beyond getting press coverage and beyond specific AI tools.

“Honeyjar can find reporters, build media lists, scan news and social, track coverage, and surface opportunities,” she said. “Those capabilities are important, but they’re just one piece of what we’re building. The bigger idea is bringing the whole communications workflow together: signals, context, strategy, judgment, timing, and execution.”

And it’s not just for founders. Masek said she’s come to realize there are “millions and millions of unassigned communicators responsible for the work of comms.”

“They don’t have the title of comms, but they’re marketers, investors, authors, creators, school superintendents, sports team leaders,” she added. “It’s incredibly horizontal, this need to nail strategic communications. It’s always passed around, but the problems are very often not solved.”

Image Credits:Honeyjar

Nor is Honeyjar trying to replace PR professionals. Masek said she and Jamshidi built the tool they wanted to use themselves. She argued that Honeyjar can make PR firms and in-house comms teams more effective, while allowing individual PR practitioners to “take on that third client without any scaling cost.”

When Honeyjar opened its waitlist, it received 10,000 signups in the first 24 hours, said Masek. Beta testers include Nextdoor, tech startup Coco Robotics, investor Bloomberg Beta, and agencies Mission North and Full Picture.

That sounds promising for companies looking to get more attention, but it could be a nightmare for journalists. We receive more pitches than we can respond to, many of them already written by AI chatbots.

When I raised my fears about getting inundated with even more PR slop, Masek noted that while Honeyjar can draft a pitch email or a social media post in the customer’s voice, the customer actually has to hit send or publish.

“We never want a world where the human is removed from the loop,” she said.

And that’s also where judgment is key. Masek said she and Jamshidi tried to “infuse and encode Honeyjar with our wisdom.” Through a broader initiative called the Comms Lab, they’re now training the product on the judgment of other PR pros as well.

“For us, judgment is knowing what to do, what not to do, when to act, and how to adapt to the situation,” Jamshidi added. “That comes from understanding a company’s goals and priorities, what’s happening inside and outside the organization, and knowing what to say, to whom, where, and when.”

In some cases, Masek said Honeyjar might even tell a founder that they’re simply not ready for coverage.

“We hear from reporters all the time who want better pitches, who want to hear from experts directly,” she said. “We actually see a future where there are more credible pitches in your inbox from sources who you actually want to hear from.”

title: Google finally releases Gemini 4 Argon
snippet: After months sitting on the sidelines of the frontier AI race, Google has finally launched its long-awaited Gemini 4 Argon model, claiming it can compete with the best the industry has to offer. Google says Argon delivers "frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows," while cutting down on hedging, repetition, and the cliches that continue to plague AI chatbots. The company claims Argon outperforms rival models like GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.5 across a range of benchmarks, including coding, cybersecurity, science, finance, and law. Google says it's already putting Argon to use internally, s … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
After months sitting on the sidelines of the frontier AI race, Google has finally launched its long-awaited Gemini 4 Argon model, claiming it can compete with the best the industry has to offer.

Google says Argon delivers “frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows,” while cutting down on hedging, repetition, and the cliches that continue to plague AI chatbots. The company claims Argon outperforms rival models like GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.5 across a range of benchmarks, including coding, cybersecurity, science, finance, and law.

Google says it’s already putting Argon to use internally, such as finding and patching cybersecurity vulnerabilities, halving the computing power needed to power YouTube’s comments section, and debugging the drone physics simulator for Alphabet’s drone delivery company Wing.

The model is rolling out today to Google’s higher-tier Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and AI mode in Search, as well to Ultra subscribers on its agentic development platform Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Argon will be available to Plus subscribers or free users.

Google is pricing Argon very competitively. The model is launching with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5 models. Even after those costs double at the end November — when the introductory period finishes — Argon will still be significantly cheaper than its frontier rivals on a per-token basis, though this doesn’t necessarily translate to lower costs in practice, as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks.

The launch fills in some of the blanks left behind from when Google first teased Argon a few weeks ago. In line with other recent frontier model releases, the public rollout follows a limited release to a select set of “trusted cyber defenders” to be tested for potential risks.

Argon is Google’s first major frontier release since Gemini 3 in late 2025. In the intervening months, impressive models from Anthropic and OpenAI have seen Google trail far behind its rivals. Seismic internal shakeups raised further doubts about the company’s ability — or desire — to reclaim its position and compete at the frontier of AI.

But Argon’s arrival suggests we can’t count Google out of the AI race just yet. Landing just a day after Meta announced its own frontier model, Muse Wonder Full, Argon is a reminder of how quickly the balance of power can shift in AI, and that the frontier is far from a two-horse race.

title: Apple’s $299 HomeView Is Ready to Take Over Your Countertops and Walls
snippet: Apple’s new smart display and speaker marks the company’s Siri AI-ification of your home. Preorders are open now.
fullText:
Apple has welcomed an entirely new product type to its ever-growing family of devices. The company unveiled the HomeView smart speaker at its Welcome Home event in New York on Tuesday — a long-rumored addition that looks like a hybrid between a HomePod and a giant Apple Watch.

The HomeView’s square screen is a 7-inch Liquid Retina display, making it quite unobstrusive. In spite of its diminutive size, this bold design choice will set Apple’s smart speaker apart from most rivals on the market, such as the Amazon Echo Show, which tend to have rectangular landscape screens.

On the front of the HomeView, a 12-megapixel camera makes use of Apple’s Center Stage technology — a zoom feature designed for video chatting, which you might be familiar with from its iPad lineup. Inside the display, two full-range drivers will help deliver room-filling Spatial Audio. The device is powered by Apple’s homegrown A18 chip — the same silicon inside the iPhone 16 Series and the MacBook Neo.

			

More from CNET

Apple’s home hub functions as a central portal for entertainment, connection and controlling your smart home devices, but also for interacting with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. This builds on the Siri AI revamp that Apple announced back at WWDC in June, which saw the company introduce a more capable, conversational voice assistant that matches up-to-date AI smarts with the company’s privacy and security standards.

“It is little surprise that the HomeView coincides with Apple’s renewed push on Siri AI and Apple Intelligence,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS, speaking from the company’s New York event. “The company has undoubtedly been waiting for the upgraded Siri experience, given how important the voice interactions are with this product.”

The HomeView will tap into information from your personal apps.Apple

Unlike most Apple devices, which are either designed completely for personal use (the iPhone or the Apple Watch) or designed to be shared by everyone in the home (the Apple TV or HomePods), the HomeView straddles both worlds. “Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing in a press release. If you don’t already use them, it sounds like it might be time to tap into shared photo albums and shared Apple Music playlists in order to make the most of the HomeView.

Apple’s HomeView will recognize your family members using built-in facial recognition, and will allow you all to check your personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders and Find My. Furthermore, when paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled device, HomeView will draw on your personal context to provide personalized answers to any questions you might ask.

Your HomeView device can either sit on your tabletop or be mounted to a wall, depending on your preference. One thing to note is that you have to decide this when you buy — either you pick the wall-mounted option or one with a domed speaker base attached. If you opt for the wall-mounted version, it can be attached using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with the option to install it yourself or have a professional do it for you.

Apple

A collection of playful and informative faces is available — some with your personal photos, others with an animated Snoopy. These faces respond dynamically to your physical and presence and movement, which sounds like a fun feature for a kitchen dance party. The idea is true personalization — whether you want interactive art, a functional interface or something in between.

Customers in the US, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand and the UK can preorder the HomeView right now for $299, with devices available from Nov. 13. It comes in silver, starlight, rose pink and space gray, so there’s bound to be at least one option that will fit your home decor scheme.

title: Apple TV 4K Gains Onboard Mics and Better Processor, but Whoa, That Price
snippet: The fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is now three times the price of Roku’s top streamer.
fullText:
Apple has unveiled its latest streaming box, the Apple TV 4K (fourth generation), which has a faster processor and onboard microphones for better integration with Siri AI. It’s coming in November for $299.

The new Apple TV has an updated A19 chip, which Apple says is 50% faster than the existing A15 processor and has twice the graphics performance. The TV 4K boasts 128GB of storage space which is the same as the previous flagship.  

The new set-top box has three onboard far-field microphones for conversing with Siri, as well as a familiar-looking remote with a traditional microphone button. The remote also includes Find My with Precision Finding if it gets lost behind the cushions.

			

More from CNET

The Apple TV 4K (fourth generation) and remote will be available in November for $299.

Connectivity includes:

Bluetooth 6

Wi‑Fi 7

HDMI 2.1

Gigabit Ethernet

All of the relevant formats are included, such as Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. You can now also create a four-speaker surround system by pairing the Apple TV 4K (fourth generation) and the new HomePod Mini 2. 

At $299, though, the Apple TV is more expensive than every other premium streaming box on the market. For instance, it’s $200 more than the Roku Ultra and the (seemingly discontinued) Google TV. The outgoing Apple TV 4K (2022) recently had a price hike of its own, with the entry-level model leaping from $129 to $199, and the company blamed the increase on an electronics shortage also known as RAMageddon.

While it’s the most expensive streamer, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is also likely to be capable, especially if you’re a gamer. The outgoing TV 4K was great for streaming games via Steam Link or Xbox Remote Play, and the new box should be even better. For everyone else, who simply want to watch TV, a $50 streamer from Amazon or Roku should do just fine.

The new Apple TV 4K is available now for preorder at Apple’s website. It’s due in stores on Nov. 13.

title: Samsung is now rolling out Android 17 to these older Galaxy devices in the US
snippet: Samsung’s One UI 9 update is now available for the Galaxy S24 and Z Fold/Flip 6, a month after the official rollout was initiated. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s One UI 9 update is now available for the Galaxy S24 and Z Fold/Flip 6, a month after the official rollout was initiated.

Samsung announced that One UI 9 is officially rolling out to devices that didn’t launch with it preloaded – i.e., the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra.

That means the Galaxy S24 series, Galaxy Z Fold 6, and Galaxy Z Flip 6 are the next to get Android 17 (via SamMobile). Of course, the rollout includes all three Galaxy S24 models. The update should appear in the settings app on those devices as a standard download.

For the time being, the update appears to be available in South Korea and the US, though it’s expected that more regions will follow within the next few days.

	

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Flip 8 were the first to get One UI 9 because Samsung switched up its update schedule a year ago. A month ago, the Galaxy S26 was given access to the new One UI 9, based on Android 17.

The update has been trickling down Samsung’s Galaxy S lineups ever since. Since the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy Z Fold 6 are just getting One UI 9, it’s expected that the Galaxy S25 and Galaxy Z Fold 5 aren’t far behind. Samsung has not updated those devices just yet.

One UI 9 includes a few notable changes, including:

My FanCam: Automatic video tracking & reframing of a subject

Generative and Editable Cards on Now Brief

Warranty and Care details in Settings menu

More Galaxy AI features: Now Nudge, Creative Studio, Interpreter, Document Scan, Voice Recorder

Privacy & security features: Security Brief, Privacy Alerts, Scam Detection

If the update isn’t ready for you yet, it should be very soon. For those on older devices, it may take a few more weeks.

title: This AI startup says it can generate permit-ready blueprints in minutes
snippet: Blueprints AI, a bootstrapped startup based in Santa Monica, developed software that produces code-compliant construction blueprints from a photo, PDF, or sketch.
fullText:
Nearly two decades ago, a young college student wrote his final thesis about software capable of generating design documents for school buildings. Al Dram was studying architecture — following in the footsteps of his parents and grandfather — but it was technology that really intrigued him.

There was just one problem: The technology his idea required didn’t exist yet.

“Then ChatGPT came along,” said Dram, recalling when OpenAI released the generative AI chatbot that uses large language models (LLMs) in November 2022.

His old idea suddenly seemed a lot more possible. Within six months, he launched the concept of Blueprints AI, a startup that uses AI to produce code-compliant and permit-ready architectural construction blueprints in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF.

Blueprints AI, which Dram officially incorporated in 2025 in Santa Monica with co-founder Coco Cao, was selected for the 2026 Startup Battlefield 200, a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place this week from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco.

During that 20-year lead-up to Blueprints AI, Dram earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture from the University of Tehran and completed two years of PhD coursework on digital design at the European Graduate School in Switzerland. He moved to the United States and opened an architecture firm in 2018 called Drams Design-Build. Then, after obtaining a general contractor’s license, he added a construction business in 2021.

Dram should have been satisfied. He wasn’t.

“I was saying, okay, maybe I can build new projects that change people’s life in that area, but it wouldn’t be a big impact,” he said. “What makes me very excited about technology is the impact, the hours saved, the energy saved of people doing the same thing over and over and over.”

Blueprints AI will unveil a more capable second-generation version of its software at Disrupt. Dram and Cao say it will make a big impact because it takes over the repetitive drafting work that fills most of an architect’s day.

“It will make better spaces for people because now architects have the time to design,” said Dram. He said architects spend about 80% of their time on drafting and only 20% on design. “I want to flip that to be 20-80.”

Dram and Cao met at an AI conference several years ago and combined their skills to build the company. Cao, a data scientist from Hong Kong, handles sales and go-to-market strategy as chief commercial officer.

The pair trained their models using eight years of approved drawing sets from Dram’s design and construction firm, which is still in business.

Its first-generation software produces architectural construction documents and costs between $3,200 and $8,500 a month, depending on the plan. Custom pricing for enterprises is also available.

The startup’s second-generation software will deliver a considerable upgrade. Customers can start with a description or sketch of a project and create blueprints for every aspect of a building at once, including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design. Version 2 allows users to design and make changes to the project, an upgrade over the first iteration. Importantly, one design change updates the entire project and is checked against local building codes.

Early customers are already using the second version, and Dram said it will become publicly available this week. The startup is already working on a third version of its software that will add in structural analysis and electrical panel design.

The technology doesn’t replace licensed architects, according to the co-founders. Licensed professionals still review the documents and affix their seal before submitting them for permits. The judgment stays human, they say.

Blueprints AI is targeting two groups with its new software. Professional architecture, engineering, and design firms make up one group, while developers and real estate owners make up another. The startup offers its software as a subscription and may add a one-time flat-fee option for those who just want it for a single project. 

To learn more about Blueprints, catch hundreds of other startups, and learn from headliners like RJ Scaringe of Rivian and Amjad Masad of Replit, join us at TechCrunch Disrupt, kicking off Tuesday in downtown San Francisco.

title: Apple’s New Smart Home Hub Is Reportedly Called HomeView and Will Ship in November
snippet: Apple is also expected to unveil a new Apple TV set-top box and HomePod Mini on Tuesday.
fullText:
The Apple smart home device that the company is expected to announce on Tuesday is called the HomeView and will ship to consumers in November, according to a report Sunday by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

The device, which will have a display and be powered by an A18 chip, will act as a Siri command center for an Apple-powered smart home, Gurman reported. The HomeView will come in two configurations: a countertop model with a metal speaker base and a wall-mounted version with a flat, square base.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

			

More from CNET

For more than a year, Apple has been rumored to be readying a Siri-focused smart display hub for the home, sometimes referred to as a HomePad. This display is expected to focus heavily on Siri AI and to compete with products such as Amazon’s Echo Show and the Google Nest Hub line by acting as a HomeKit hub.

Alongside the HomeView, Apple is expected to unveil a new Apple TV set-top box powered by an A19 chip and an updated HomePod Mini with an S10 chip that extends voice control, music playback and other functionality throughout the household, Gurman reported.

Apple is expected to unveil the devices at its “Welcome Home” smart home event Tuesday. Invitations went out on Thursday with a distinctive rainbow-colored Apple logo.

The HomeView is expected to ship in mid-November, Gurman wrote.

title: Report: HomePod mini 2 to release on October 30 with these upgrades
snippet: In just a couple days, Apple should be unveiling its long-awaited new lineup of new Home products. That includes an updated HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, the brand-new smart home hub called ‘HomeView’, as well as a new lineup of smart home accessories, in collaboration with LG. Here’s what to expect with the HomePod mini 2. more…
fullText:
In just a couple days, Apple should be unveiling its long-awaited new lineup of new Home products. That includes an updated HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, the brand-new smart home hub called ‘HomeView’, as well as a new lineup of smart home accessories, in collaboration with LG. Here’s what to expect with the HomePod mini 2.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the new HomePod mini should equip the S10 chip, up from the current S5 chip. This isn’t quite the latest silicon, but it’s still a massive step-change from the outgoing model.

With the S10 chip, the HomePod mini will be able to offer Siri AI features – a first for any of Apple’s Home products. It’ll also “extend” your HomeView throughout your house, with voice control and music playback all being able to sync up to your HomeView. Of course, the updated Apple TV and HomeView will also support Siri AI.

The new HomePod mini will come in a fresh array of colors, including pink, green, and blue – on top of the traditional midnight and white.

Outside of the S10 chip, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to offer Apple’s N1 networking chip to serve as a Thread and Matter radio, as well as offering Wi-Fi 7 support. Currently, the HomePod mini only offers Wi-Fi 4.

Pricing and release date

	

While pricing isn’t necessarily clear, it’s worth noting that HomePod mini increased in price from $99 to $129 back in June with Apple’s wave of memory-related price hikes. I personally expect pricing to stay the same, as Apple likely anticipated the upcoming hardware when it set them. Only time will tell, though.

As for release date, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that the second-generation HomePod mini should arrive in stores on October 30th, alongside the new Apple TV 4K. The HomeView, on the other hand, is expected to slip into mid-November. You can read more about the HomeView here.

title: Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17
snippet: Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update. more…
fullText:
Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update.

What’s new in Android 17 on Samsung Galaxy?

One UI 9, Samsung’s Android 17 update, continues the trend of evolution more than overhaul. The update introduces some slight design tweaks, more AI-powered features, and other changes built on the redesign that debuted in One UI 7 and was iterated in last year’s Android 16-based One UI 8. 

Some key changes in One UI 9 include:

Warranty & Samsung Care status in the Settings menu

Broader support for Now Nudge

My FanCam automatic video cropping based on a select subject

More Quick Panel (quick settings) customization

AI privacy alerts

Upgrades to Samsung DeX

New lock screen clocks that can adapt to your wallpaper

Samsung Galaxy devices with Android 17 – The full list

While Samsung hasn’t confirmed an exact schedule for its One UI 9 and Android 17 rollout for Galaxy devices, there are updates now rolling out in parts of the globe. Below you’ll find a regularly-updated list of every Samsung Galaxy device that has received a stable Android 17 update so far.

	

Galaxy S devices with Android 17

Galaxy S26

Galaxy S26+

Galaxy S26 Ultra

Galaxy S25 (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25+ (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25 Ultra (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy S25 Edge (limited availability)

Galaxy S24 (limited availability)

Galaxy S24+ (limited availability)

Galaxy S24 Ultra (limited availability)

Galaxy Z devices with Android 17

Galaxy Z Fold 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy Z TriFold (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Fold 6 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 6 (limited availability)

Galaxy A devices with Android 17

Galaxy A57 (limited availability)

Updating…

One UI 9 changelog

Here’s the full changelog from Samsung for One UI 9, as listed for the Galaxy S26 series. Some features may vary by device.

Galaxy AI

Enhanced Now nudge

Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.

Focus on someone important

My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.

Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you

In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.

See useful information during calls

See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.

Productivity and multitasking

More customizable quick panel

You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.

Privacy, security, and device protection

Warranty and care

The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.

Lock down your phone quickly

It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.

Location access transparency

Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.

Stronger security and privacy protection

Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.

AI privacy alerts

Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.

Samsung Health

New look for Samsung Health

Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.

Customize your Health home screen

Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.

Log health data quickly

It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.

Advanced trend analysis

Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.

Monitor changes in your sleep vitals

Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.

Manage your heart health

Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.

Track your cardio load

See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.

Check your fitness index

Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.

Keep your ears safe

The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.

View your cycle and body rhythm

Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.

Bixby

Activate Bixby with a gesture

Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.

Manage your conversations

Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.

Bixby on the Home screen

Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.

Accessibility

Discover new Accessibility features

Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.

Text spotlight for easier reading

Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.

Physical keyboard shortcuts

Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.

Mouse keys enhancements

New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.

Replace swipe with single tap

The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.

Select to speak

Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.

Improved TalkBack updates

TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.

Even more improvements

New Lock screen clock

title: Apple gets a $360 price target from JP Morgan despite iPhone demand concerns
snippet: Just days after Apple’s stock took a hit over reports of iPhone 18 Pro production cuts, JP Morgan has raised its AAPL price target by $20. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Just days after Apple’s stock took a hit over reports of iPhone 18 Pro production cuts, JP Morgan has raised its AAPL price target by $20. Here are the details.

iPhone Duo to help offset staggered release window

Last Friday, Nikkei Asia reported that, according to “multiple people familiar with the matter,” Apple had told select suppliers to cut component production for the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.”

The report sent Apple shares down roughly 2.5% in early trading, although the stock has recovered much of that loss and closed at $340.97 today.

That said, JP Morgan released a new investor note today (via AppleInsider), arguing that the reported cuts are consistent with Apple’s usual production patterns and don’t necessarily point to an unexpected drop in demand.

The report also comments on Apple’s staggered iPhone launch schedule, with JP Morgan expecting the iPhone Duo to offset the sales shortfall caused by the absence of the regular iPhone 18, which is expected to hit shelves early next year.

Interestingly, earlier today, a separate report from China’s Securities Times claimed that Apple had increased its iPhone Duo orders by 30%, potentially bringing its production for the remainder of 2026 close to 10 million units.

Looking ahead to the December quarter, JP Morgan expects Apple to sell 8.5 million iPhone Duo units. JP Morgan also projects a roughly 2% decline in iPhone revenue year-over-year, but a 2% increase in Apple’s overall revenue.

The firm also continues to flag supply constraints and broader economic pressures that could affect consumer demand.

All in all, JP Morgan raised its AAPL price target from $340 to $360, while maintaining its Overweight rating on the stock.

We broke the news this week that a next-gen Google TV Streamer is incoming, but it also arrives as Google’s smart home hardware strategy faces a tough spot and new competition.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Google’s smart home efforts have been a bit sporadic over the years. 2021 seemed like a turning point as the company rebooted its Nest camera lineup, but it was followed by a good bout of silence. That was broken up by the occasional new camera, streaming device, and the Google Home Speaker earlier this year, but it’s all felt rather unfocused and unpredictable.

And that leads into this week’s news: Google has a new TV Streamer coming.

	

This next-gen release is pretty similar on paper, though with the additions of far-field microphones, presence sensing, and a new remote. 

Next-gen Google TV Streamer in the works with microphones, presence sensing, & new remote

Sounds good! 

But, at the same time, it feels like Google should have much bigger priorities in its smart home ecosystem. Those aforementioned 2021 Nest cameras are still in need of refreshes. The 2K updates for the wired cameras have been welcome upgrades, but I do wish my battery-powered models had the same quality. The Nest Hub Max is way overdue for an update at this point, and I’d argue that should have been the priority over a new audio speaker. Google Home has done a great job over the past couple of years at building out a third-party ecosystem of smart home devices, but the first-party hardware has been lacking, and there’s not enough tight integration with most third-party hardware to bridge the gap.

So while I’m all for a new Google TV Streamer, I’m also struggling to feel like this is the release we should be seeing right now. 

Especially in the context of this week’s other news. Apple is making a big smart home play. On top of the “HomePad” smart display, the company is teaming up with LG for some second-party hardware with deep integration. Putting aside that Google has really dropped the ball on its massive lead in the smart display space, integrations like these are exactly what I wish Google Home saw more of. Walmart cameras, the Yale smart lock, and the First Alert smoke alarms are a good start, but there’s so much room for more.

As a fan and a genuine user of Google’s smart home ecosystem, I really feel like Google is leaving so much out there right now. Just me? Let’s discuss!

Amazon did the thing!

Well I never thought this day would come. After well over a decade of Fire Tablets that were inherently limited, Amazon this week announced new “Alexa” tablets that have the Google Play Store installed. Wild times folks, wild times.

fullText:
The wall connector adds at least another $59 to the $299 HomeView price.﻿

The wall connector adds at least another $59 to the $299 HomeView price.﻿

by  Jess Weatherbed

Oct 13, 2026, 3:48 PM UTC

Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

The HomeView smart home display announced by Apple today comes in two models that both cost $299: one with a speaker base, and the other being a self explanatory “Wall Mounted” version. If you want the latter, however, you’ll actually have to pay at least $59 more — the mounts required to actually affix the display to your wall are sold separately. Maybe calling it the “Mountless” version would have been more accurate?

Apple isn’t exactly shouting about that sneaky additional premium for wall-mounted HomeView customers. The details are mentioned in the small print at the bottom of the product announcement page:

HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (US), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (US), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (US).

It also becomes apparent when you go through the process of adding the HomeView to your basket on Apple’s webstore. You’re asked to choose from the available mount options (which doesn’t include the Power Mount PoE Wired yet) which each bump up that $299 price, or select “No mount” to proceed with no extra charge — but Apple clearly states on this option that the “HomeView (Wall Mounted) requires a mount and power solution to operate.”

Given it doesn’t ship with a power source, you can’t have the wall model HomeView leaning against something or laying on a flat surface to evade the extra cost. You also can’t buy the desktop model that doesn’t have any additional requirements and keep the speaker base aside because it can’t be converted into the wall version. They’re two distinct versions, and the wall option only comes in two colors. Presumably some third-party manufacturers will release more affordable wall mount options in time, but either way, folks who want to wall mount their HomeView will pay a premium over those who opt for the desktop model.

title: GTA 6 Blamed for PlayStation Pro 5 Shortages
snippet: The game’s exclusivity is leading to greater demand for the high-end console.
fullText:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is the most-anticipated game of 2026, and it’s already being blamed for gaming console shortages, especially the PlayStation 5 Pro. The high-end Sony console is currently out of stock on Sony.com and is selling on auction sites for $1,100 and over.

Part of the reason for high console demand is that GTA 6 will be exclusive to PlayStation 5/Pro and Xbox Series X/S when it comes out on Nov. 19, and no other platforms have been announced yet.

In September, Sony reportedly advised distributors that the PlayStation 5 Pro would be in short supply until 2027, citing “temporary market supply constraints and high demand.” The most severe bottleneck limiting PlayStation distribution is a global crisis in memory and storage components driven by the AI infrastructure squeeze, or RAMageddon. 

			

More from CNET

The PS 5 Pro promises better frame rates for a number of games as well as enhanced 4K processing, while the Rockstar Studios game is also designed to work on the “vanilla” PS5.

Yet, GTA 6 isn’t the only recent high-profile PlayStation release: The PS5-exclusive Wolverine — by the makers of Spider-Man and Spider-Man 2 — has reportedly sold 2.16 million copies since September.

The PlayStation 5 Pro debuted in November 2024 for $700, but its retail price has since increased to $900.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is the long-awaited sequel to Grand Theft Auto 5, which first appeared in 2013. The crime-based game reportedly offers a playable area twice the size of the previous game’s. It’s available for preorder for $80.

Representatives for Sony did not respond immediately to CNET’s request for more information.

fullText:
Tom Warren

 

is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

When Nvidia originally showed off DLSS 5 earlier this year, the technology immediately got branded as gen AI for video games. To gamers, Nvidia had lost the plot. I personally couldn’t get over how faces were transformed using DLSS 5. The 15-year-old student from Hogwarts Legacy suddenly looked much older, and Grace from Resident Evil Requiem looked yassified.

Now more than six months later, DLSS 5 is about to debut properly in Hogwarts Legacy, and it looks like it has been seriously toned down. Nvidia published new comparison screenshots today, where the changes to faces are as subtle as they are in NBA 2K27. Teenagers no longer look like middle-aged men, and even the environmental changes look more subtle.

Nvidia’s DLSS 5 in Hogwarts Legacy in March.

Nvidia’s new Hogwarts Legacy DLSS 5 comparisons.

Nvidia has always maintained that developers have “detailed artistic control” over DLSS 5, and ultimately make the choice on how to implement the technology in their own games. DLSS 5 will now appear in Hogwarts Legacy on November 5th, and it’s also coming to Where Winds Meet late next month.

Nvidia is also improving the performance hit of DLSS 5 with an October update to the neural rendering system that should make it twice as fast on RTX 50-series GPUs and the upcoming RTX Spark laptops. “The DLSS 5 October update shrinks the footprint by 24 percent to roughly 118 million parameters while reducing 4K VRAM usage by 20 percent,” says Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes. This new DLSS 5 model will debut first in NBA 2K27 on October 16th and “will ship by default with future DLSS 5 games.”

Alongside the DLSS 5 updates, Nvidia has also shipped a new Nvidia app beta update that includes a faster performance mode for Frame Generation on RTX 40- and 50-series GPUs. The updated AI model uses a “faster and lighter algorithm to boost frame rates” for Frame Gen, Multi Frame Gen, and Dynamic Multi Frame Gen. Nvidia says it has “minor trade-offs in image quality,” and that performance mode for Frame Generation should now be up to 35 precent faster.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Onvis releases a Matter over Thread outdoor smart plug with energy monitoring
snippet: Onvis has released a new outdoor smart plug that checks all the boxes you’d want in an outdoor smart plug: Matter over Thread, real-time energy monitoring, and IP65 weather resistance. If you’ve been looking for an outdoor plug that works natively with Apple Home without a hub of its own, this is a great option as you think outdoor lighting for Christmas, etc. more…
fullText:
Onvis has released a new outdoor smart plug that checks all the boxes you’d want in an outdoor smart plug: Matter over Thread, real-time energy monitoring, and IP65 weather resistance. If you’ve been looking for an outdoor plug that works natively with Apple Home without a hub of its own, this is a great option as you think outdoor lighting for Christmas, etc.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Most of your outdoor smart plugs that work with Apple HomeKit over Wi-Fi depend on your router’s signal reaching outside, which depending on what your house is made out of (mine is brick for example, so Wi-Fi outdoors can be rough). Thread is a mesh protocol in which devices route traffic through one another, making it more reliable for outdoor locations that might be on the edge of your Wi-Fi coverage. Onvis built this plug on top Matter over Thread, so it works with Apple Home, Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and SmartThings without being locked into any single smart home platform. You do need a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K to take full advantage of it, though.

Energy monitoring

A really nice feature for this plug is that it tracks real-time power usage and energy consumption through your Matter-compatible smart home system, so you can see exactly how much electricity your landscape lighting, pool pump, or outdoor heater is using. That data appears directly in Apple Home’s energy view without requiring a separate app as well.

Onvis’s outdoor smart plug is rated IP65, which means that it’s protected against dust and low-pressure water jets (from sprinklers or rain). It handles up to 1800 watts, which is enough for landscape lighting, holiday decorations, outdoor fans, etc. Schedules and automations work natively inside of Apple Home, so you can set landscape lights to turn on at sunset and off at a specific time without building anything complicated.

Wrap up

Onvis is filling a nice product gap at a good price point with its new outdoor plug that has Matter over Thread, energy monitoring, etc. If you’ve been waiting to buy an outdoor plug that has all the modern smart home tech built in, this is a great pickup. They’ve been a solid vendor for Apple Home for years as well. 

The Onvis Outdoor Smart Plug is available now on Amazon.

title: Galaxy phones reportedly ‘yield no profit at all’ when sold as Samsung cuts production
snippet: A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%. more…
fullText:
A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%.

Korean media, MoneyToday, reports that Samsung is cutting Galaxy smartphone production by up to 30% through Q4 2026. Where original forecasts expected Samsung to produce around 270 million smartphones in 2026, the company may just barely surpass 200 million at this point.

The reason for the reduction is, of course, the surging price of memory. 

	

Despite Samsung’s major role within the memory market, Samsung Mobile still has to deal with the same downsides as other manufacturers. The report points out that 12GB of RAM has jumped in price by 175% since last year and, in Q3 and Q4, it’s expected to rise by around 20% compared to the previous quarter alone. Samsung’s Q4 is generally a bit quiet as the lead-up to 2027 flagships looms and as other launches start to age out.

	

The big kicker here is that Samsung is apparently making “no profit at all” when it sells a Galaxy smartphone. This is presumably a layered statement, as one would imagine that more expensive devices like the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Galaxy Z Fold 8 still manage some level of profit, but even if it’s just a general statement about the whole lineup, it certainly explains Samsung’s recent price hikes. Samsung’s mobile division is expected to mount a 19 trillion won loss in Q3 2026, the report brings out, which is around $14 billion USD.

AI is just great, isn’t it.

Discovery Plus is raising prices across its ad-free and ad-supported plans. Starting Tuesday, the ad-supported plan will go from $5.99 to $6.99 / month, while the ad-free tier will jump from $9.99 to $11.99 / month.

The price hike comes just one week after Paramount closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owned Discovery Plus and HBO Max. The combined companies, known as Skydance, plan to merge Paramount Plus and HBO Max into “a single service over time,” though it’s not clear whether Discovery Plus will remain a standalone streamer.

Discovery Plus streams shows from networks like TLC, The Discovery Channel, HGTV, Food Network, and Investigation Discovery. Many shows from the platform are also included within an HBO Max subscription, such as 90 Day Fiancé, Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives, and Deadliest Catch. Discovery Plus last raised prices in January 2025.

This latest Discovery Plus price increase will go into effect immediately for new subscribers, while existing ones will see the increase in their next billing statement on or after November 12th.

fullText:
Update, October 7: Apple has now released both RCs to public beta testers as well. The build numbers are unchanged from the developer RCs.

In addition to releasing macOS 27.2 Golden Gate public beta 2, Apple is now rolling out the first Release Candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2. Here are the details.

Security updates continue for older macOS versions

As is usually the case for point updates of older macOS versions, Apple today rolled out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, without first releasing regular beta versions.

Apple released macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 late last month, both of which saw two RCs before the official rollout.

Apple’s release notes for the first macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RCs mention only that they “provide[s] important security fixes and [are] recommended for all users.” Last month’s updates contained a single CoreGraphics security fix, with its details reading:

Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.

Apple will likely detail the fixes included in macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 after their official release, which will likely come alongside macOS 27.2 Golden Gate within the next few weeks.

The release build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 RC 1 is 24H219, while the release build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RC 1 is 25G320.
