title: Apple and Epic clash over document production in latest App Store court filing
snippet: Epic Games is accusing Apple of “manufacturing” a pause in the legal proceedings over its proposed new App Store commission rates. Apple disagrees. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Epic Games is accusing Apple of “manufacturing” a pause in the legal proceedings over its proposed new App Store commission rates. Apple disagrees. Here are the details.

In a joint status update, Epic Games and Apple present very different accounts of Apple’s efforts to turn over internal documents explaining how it arrived at its proposed App Store commission rates.

A bit of context

As a reminder, in August, Apple proposed a new commission structure for purchases made through external App Store links.

Under the proposed structure, developers would pay commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, down from the 27% fee Apple introduced in 2024 after a court ordered the company to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods.

The court later found Apple in contempt of its order, a designation Apple is seeking to overturn before the Supreme Court, arguing that the order never forbade it from charging any commissions at all.

While the Supreme Court considers Apple’s challenge to the contempt ruling, a lower court is separately examining whether Apple can impose commissions on purchases made through external links, and if so, how much it can charge.

Apple recently tried to pause those proceedings until the Supreme Court reached a decision, but its requests were rejected by both the lower court and the Supreme Court.

As part of that process, Apple submitted its proposed 5% to 15% commission structure in August, along with evidence supporting those rates.

Under the agreement governing the proceedings, Apple was also required to hand over internal documents showing how it arrived at those rates.

The documents are meant to give Epic an opportunity to examine the basis for Apple’s proposed fees before formally responding to the court.

That’s where the latest dispute comes in, with Epic accusing Apple of deliberately delaying the proceedings and Apple rejecting those allegations.

Apple and Epic dispute evidence behind proposed App Store fees

In the joint status filing, Epic says that “[n]early two months after its production deadline, Apple has scarcely produced any documents,” adding that “Apple’s […] continued unwillingness to commit to a date certain by which it will complete its production demonstrates that Court intervention is essential.”

Apple disputes those accusations, arguing that it had already fulfilled its initial obligation to produce documents explaining how it arrived at the proposed rates.

The company also blames Epic for the delays, saying the Fortnite maker took weeks to submit additional document requests, and subsequently demanded extensive searches involving 27 individuals. Apple says it has agreed to those requests and expects to substantially complete its production by November 25.

In the document, Epic also disputes Apple’s assertions that only four senior executives were involved in determining the proposed commission rates, those four executives being Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Kevan Parekh, and Carson Oliver.

Epic argues that the decision was also informed by discussions and analyses conducted by other teams within Apple, including work on alternative commission structures in markets outside the United States. (And speaking of that, there is also a dispute over whether Epic should have access to documents concerning Apple’s international commission policies.)

Apple, in turn, maintains that the decision-making process was much narrower than the one behind its original 27% commission, and relied heavily on analyses conducted by outside experts rather than broader internal discussions.

Apple says it has already provided the business records and data that informed its proposal, and disputes Epic’s assertion that a larger group of employees must have been involved in determining the new rates.

Throughout its rebuttal of Epic’s accusations, Apple repeatedly emphasizes that it has agreed to Epic’s requests for additional documents and broader searches, arguing that the scope of those demands, and the time Epic took to make them, are responsible for the delays.

Apple also says Epic caught it by surprise by asking the court to impose a November 1 deadline for completing document production, rather than first discussing that deadline with Apple. The company makes a similar argument about Epic’s objections to the scope of the documents Apple agreed to produce, saying Epic should have raised those concerns directly before seeking court intervention.

Epic, on the other hand, says “Apple feigns surprise at every request Epic raises, as if the Parties, this Court, Magistrate Judge Hixson, and three Court-appointed special masters did not just recently complete a months-long process to extract from Apple documents Epic was clearly entitled to receive.”

For this reason, Epic asks the court to order Apple to:

“[I]mmediately begin rolling document productions and fully complete its productions on a reasonable timeline, and by no later than November 1, 2026”

“[P]roduce by said deadline all relevant documents, without regard to the artificial limitations Apple has placed on the scope of its production, as further detailed [in the document].”

title: MacBook Pro overhaul: entry-level model to gain new design sooner than expected
snippet: Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected.

Normally, when Apple introduces a new MacBook Pro design, it takes a while to trickle down. For instance, the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M1 Pro and M1 Max was introduced in 2021, but the base model MacBook Pro stuck with the 13-inch design until 2023, when it gained the 14-inch chassis with the M3 chip.

Similarly, when Apple redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2016, it wasn’t until 2019 that the entry level model gained the Touch Bar. There’s also a similar story for the 2012 retina MacBook Pro redesign.

This time around though, there’ll only be a roughly 6 month gap before the redesign comes to the entry level.

M7 entry-level with redesign

According to Bloomberg, Apple will be introducing the redesign to the entry level MacBook Pro in early 2027, shortly after debuting it in the high end MacBook Pros, rumored to be called MacBook Ultra. From the report:

Apple is also preparing a revamped entry-level MacBook Pro, code-named K104, for as early as the first half of next year. The 14-inch laptop will adopt a new design in line with what Apple is preparing for higher-end MacBooks with touch screens due between the end of this year and early next year.

It’s worth noting that there’ll also be another entry level MacBook Pro with the current design and the M6 chip, which is currently on track to debut this fall alongside the redesigned high-end MacBook Pros. 

To make things even weirder, those redesigned high-end MacBook Pros are also expected to debut with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, instead of M6 generation chips. Apple recently made a decision to abandon its plans for high end M6 chips to instead accelerate M7.

In short, it’ll look like this:

Fall 2026: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M6/old design, high-end with M5 Pro/Max and new design

Spring 2027: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M7 and new design

Fall 2027: High-end MacBook Pro refresh with M7 Pro/M7 Max

Of course, the redesign is expected to feature a slightly thinner chassis, OLED displays with touch support, and possibly even come with a Dynamic Island.

Wrap up

With the recent price hikes, this is excellent news for some people. I’m sure the redesigned 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro will likely cost over $2500, so if you’re looking to get something more in budget with the M7 chip and the redesign, you’ll only have to wait until the following spring.

	

It’s certainly unfortunate that the $1,999 price point of the entry level MacBook Pro today is what the Pro chip versions cost just under a year ago, but that’s the inevitable reality of this memory shortage.

Are you looking forward to the M7 MacBook Pro with the redesign? Let us know in the comments.

title: Googlebook improving ‘Better Together’ Android sync features, Samsung support rolling out
snippet: The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices. more…
fullText:
The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices.

There are several core features that work between Android phones and Googlebook including app streaming, notification sync, “Continue On” for compatible apps, and more. But, at launch, not everything works as expected. Some features, like Instant Hotspot, seem to work widely, but others are either inconsistent, slow to activate, or simply unavailable. One of the problems is that it takes a bit of work to fully activate these features.

In a post on Reddit, Google explains that it has started rolling out “smoother first-time setup” for these features, reducing the needed steps to actually set up these cross-device features. A bug where the QR code used to pair your phone continues to show even after Googlebook pairing is complete is apparently also fixed with this update. Google Play Services 26.37 (on the phone) is the version you’re looking for. You can check for Play Services updates through the Play Store. Cross-device Services also needs to be updated to 1.0.1346, again through the Play Store. 

Apparently, these updates also seem to enable support for Samsung devices. 

	

Missing Galaxy smartphone support was perhaps the biggest gap in Googlebook at launch, at least in terms of compatibility. Google originally said this would arrive “in the coming weeks,” a phrase that continues to be incredibly vague.

Here’s Google’s full breakdown of everything you’re looking for:

Confirm your phone runs Android 17: Your Android phone must run Android 17. To check your version, open Settings > About phone > Android version (your phone’s settings may vary). Better Together features work with Pixel and compatible Android 17 phones including Xiaomi, Oppo, OnePlus, Motorola, Lenovo, Honor, Sharp, Sony, Samsung (One UI 9.0), and more.

Check your Bluetooth and Wi-Fi: Confirm your phone and Googlebook use the same personal Google Account with both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on.

Use a private home Wi-Fi network: Hotel, cafe, office, and guest Wi-Fi networks frequently use client isolation, which blocks direct local connections between your phone and laptop. Pause any active VPNs or network DNS blockers and test on a standard home Wi-Fi network.

Update Google Play services: Google Play services must be at version 26.37 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings > Apps (or Apps & notifications)> See all apps. If Google Play services doesn’t appear, select More and then Show system. Select Google Play services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Update Cross-device services: Cross-device services must be at version 1.0.1346 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings, then Apps (or Apps & notifications), then See all apps. Select Cross-device services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Verify Continue activity sub-toggles: On your phone under Settings, search for Cross-device services > Continue activity, and confirm that Tasks, Apps, Notifications, Files & media sharing are all turned On. 

Restart both your phone and your Googlebook to ensure changes take effect.

Some Samsung Galaxy users have already confirmed that “Better Together” features are working on their Googlebooks following these updates.

Missing Samsung support was initially attributed to missing updates on Samsung’s end by some, but it sounds like everything is worked out at this point. You’ll still need One UI 9, though, which is only rolled out to a small portion of Samsung’s device catalog at this point.

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

title: Google starts rolling out its upgraded Pixel screen savers to the Pixel 9
snippet: When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets. more…
fullText:
When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets.

A select group of users are starting to spot these screensavers being added to older Pixels, beginning with the Pixel 9, as reported by Android Authority. Earlier Pixels did have support for a basic screensaver tool, but with this upgrade, every option available on Google’s latest releases have finally been backported to its 2024 hardware. The update appears to include a pop-up demo of these new options, along with everything currently available as of the Pixel 11’s launch. Clock, Charge, Weather, Photos, and Home Controls are all available, and can be swiped through at will. And speaking of Charge, it too seems to be headed to the Pixel 10 series, after having been exclusive to the Pixel 11 for the past two months.

Unfortunately, it does seem like this is one of Google’s classic slow rollouts. There aren’t a massive amount of reports from Pixel 9 users that these styles are live on their devices, implying it might take a few weeks before reaching everyone. The same goes for Charge on the Pixel 10, with plenty of Redditors confirming they have yet to see that specific style arrive.

title: XREAL Aura with Android XR start at $1,279
snippet: XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279. more…
fullText:
XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279.

XREAL makes glasses that aren’t a traditional VR headset, nor are they the smart glasses we’ve imagined for the future. They sit somewhere in between, with a display that sits atop a see-through lens so you can mix the display’s content with the real world around you, no cameras needed. 

As we noted in a review of XREAL One Pro, though, the base experience of using the glasses to display content from a USB-C device like a laptop, phone, or handheld game console is a bit limited. Android XR’s promises are set to deliver a big upgrade to the experience, and that’s exactly what XREAL has been building.

XREAL Aura is effectively the same core idea, just with an included puck that has a battery, processing power, and Android XR. And it starts at $1,279, the company has today confirmed. The price of XREAL Aura was the missing puzzle piece for months, and it’s actually well below the company’s promise of “under $1,500.”

	

That’s for the base 12GB/256GB model, with an upgraded version costing a bit more:

XREAL Aura 12GB/256GB: $1,279

XREAL Aura 16GB/512GB: $1,499

There’s no charge for the medium or large size difference.

As far as actually putting in an order, XREAL says the initial delivery wave will arrive “before the holidays,” with a second wave presumably arriving sometime in early 2027. You have to purchase a $199 “Priority Deposit” to place a pre-order, with the cost going towards the price of your Aura glasses.

Pre-orders open later this month.

title: Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android
snippet: After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards. more…
fullText:
After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards.

The previous design made use of a carousel to show your stored payment methods. This design showed just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google allowed you to reorder cards and set a default one.

	

With this stacked redesign, the homepage shows one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen layout that shows most of each card. “Manage payment methods” at the bottom lets you arrange the order and set the default.

You select a card to tap-to-pay. To see card details and transaction history, there’s a new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This adds an extra step compared to the previous approach.

	

This approach is nice for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom. There are no other changes to the Google Wallet homepage.

This redesign started appearing in September and is now seeing broader availability. It’s rolling out via a server-side update and appeared on several devices we checked today.

title: ‘HomePad’ is coming next week, with three features I’ve long wanted
snippet: Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for.

#1: Apple Photos on a digital picture frame

Digital picture frames are nothing new. But I’ve never owned one, in large part for two reasons:

All my pictures live in Apple Photos

I don’t want to manually add pictures to the digital frame

There are currently zero digital picture frames with native Apple Photos integration for an effort-free experience. But with the HomePad, rumors indicate there’s a Photos face available that will automatically cycle through pictures from Apple Photos.

This is exactly what I’ve been wanting for years. I hope to put several HomePads throughout the house so they can surprise and delight me with memories at every turn (while providing other key features too).

#2: Apple Music in the home with lyrics onscreen

I own a few HomePods, and enjoy listening to music with them. But what I’ve really wanted for a long time is the chance to see lyrics while listening.

Thanks to AirPlay, I can do this with my iPhone while music plays through the HomePod. I rarely do this, though, because I try to avoid pulling my phone out as much as possible with family around.

With HomePad though, all signs point to the Music app letting you view lyrics onscreen while a song is playing. I’m terrible at picking up lyrics just by ear, so I’m excited for the chance to better learn songs while staying in the moment with family members when we’re listening together.

#3: Siri AI in a HomePod-like device with a display

	

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri. Unlike the old Siri on my HomePods, Siri AI can handle basically any question you throw at it. And with the HomePad, not only will Siri’s intelligence get a boost—it will also be able to show visuals in its responses.

I ask Siri on my HomePods to do basic things like set reminders, or provide info on the weather. But with Siri AI on the HomePad, I imagine I’ll turn to Siri far more often than I ever have. That’s already been true with Siri AI on my iPhone.

Having Apple’s new AI assistant all throughout the house, and equipped with a display for showing visual results, should prove a big improvement from my current HomePod setup.

title: Googlebook’s hidden ‘Glowbar Disco’ turns your laptop’s lid into a light show — how to find it
snippet: Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank. more…
fullText:
Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank.

The Glowbar on Googlebook is a carryover from the iconic light bar on the original Chromebook Pixel. It doesn’t function quite the same, lacking the fun and useful “knock knock” gesture that Google’s original offered, but it still shows battery on plug-in, and serves as a nice accent too.

But, hidden behind the scenes is more control over the glowbar.

The “Glowbar Disco” app is an Easter egg buried deep within the OS, and even Google’s Alexander Kuscher admits it might be “too hard to find.” The app itself lets you set the Glowbar on a Googlebook to show a constant color, a preset animation, a gradient of colors, or even sync with music. It leaves the Glowbar active whenever the machine is turned on and the Disco app is open, and it’s a super fun little addition.

	

Finding the app, though, is not exactly an easy task. 

You’ll have to go to Settings > Apps then allow the search function to show system apps, then search for “Glowbar Disco.” From there you can launch the app, but you’ll need to repeat that process every time you want to access it. And, if you close the app, the effects stop.

If you ask me, this should be baked into the Settings because it is very fun. Hopefully that’ll change in time — Googlebooks certainly need a lot of updates.

title: Someone ported Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text to other Android phones
snippet: One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is. more…
fullText:
One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is.

Rambler on the Pixel 11 series is essentially AI-enhanced voice-to-text. The feature takes what you say and runs it through AI, spitting out a result that includes grammar and formatting while taking out filler words and times you may have tripped over your words. It’s not perfect, as not being able to see a live preview or get word-for-word output can be a little unsettling, but it’s still a huge upgrade to traditional voice-to-text.

That’s why it can be a little annoying that it’s Pixel 11-only.

A developer, though, has managed to port the feature to any other Android phone. “PixelBoard” is a split off of the Gboard app that brings support for Rambler to essentially any other Android phone. 

	
	

In a post on Reddit (h/t Artem Russakovskii), the developer explains that the project is based on the official Gboard app, just modified to unlock Rambler and other new writing tools.

The app is available for sideloading via the project’s GitHub page, but as always that’s done at your own risk. That said, we installed the app on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 to a complete success. It runs just like Rambler on a Pixel 11. Your results may vary and, again, install at your own risk! The project has other install methods available, including patching the existing Gboard installation on your phone.

It’s still unclear if Google ever plans to bring Rambler to other devices, but third-party mods like this will be the only way to do so for the time being. For those wanting to stick with a Play Store install, Microsoft’s SwiftKey acts as a fine alternative.

title: Google Wallet for Android getting vertically stacked card list [U]
snippet: Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list. more…
fullText:
Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list.

Update 10/6: This revamp is not yet widely rolled out, but we’re slowly seeing it on more devices.

With this stacked redesign, you’ll see one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you can tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen view (as seen below). After selecting a card, you can tap-to-pay.

To see card details and transaction history, select the new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This is more cumbersome than the current design. 

	

Original 9/14: The current design shows your saved credit and debit cards as a carousel at the top of the screen. You swipe horizontally to browse, with this approach showing just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google lets you reorder the payment methods and set a default card. This interface allows passes to share the homepage.

The new design uses a vertical list, like the Wallet app on iPhone, that really benefits those with multiple saved cards. Google is showing much more of the card design than Apple, which is a nice aspect of the current look.

This approach is definitely friendlier for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom.

There are a handful of reports about this rollout over the weekend, with most coming from international users.

snippet: Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details.

Apple’s partnership with The King’s Trust dates back to 2019

In a Newsroom post published today, Apple and The King’s Trust announced the “Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs” initiative, which will “offer young people meaningful engagement with Apple experts across industries as they explore a variety of career pathways, equipping them with the technology, resources, skills, confidence, and expertise needed to realize their potential.”

According to Apple, the program’s immersive educational experience began earlier this week with “music industry and creative workshops, aligned to the recent opening of Apple Music Hall.”

“At Apple, we believe education is a powerful force for equity and opportunity. Jonathan Townsend, The King’s Trust’s UK chief executive, also commented on the initiative, calling it “an exciting new chapter in our partnership that will help even more young people develop the confidence and creative digital skills they need to take their next steps toward employment.”

title: Why did it take so long for someone to make a magnetic USB-C port? [Video]
snippet: In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything. more…
fullText:
In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is a full-on powerhouse with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chipset, up to 128GB of RAM, and plenty of ports. But it’s one of those ports that is the most unique new features.

“Magnetic Connect” is Microsoft’s name for “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C” charging port. The USB-C port itself functions as normal with any standard cable, but the included charger is specially designed to magnetically attach akin to Apple’s MagSafe or any other number of magnetic charging connectors.

I want it.

	

The “how” here is that the charging portion of the cable uses super-strong magnets to align and latch on the charger so the port connects properly, but the charger itself also tapers the edges of the USB-C port so it can more easily slide into place. As such, that end won’t securely connect to your phone or other devices, as it needs that magnet to hold itself in place. 

	

The Verge shows it in action in a video on YouTube:

Microsoft is apparently hoping this idea will catch on and show up on other laptops, and I sure hope that’s the case! As for phones, the size of the magnets implies it probably won’t be feasible in a standard smartphone, but I really hope this idea starts showing up everywhere! Certainly I hope it at least shows up on a laptop that doesn’t cost $2,600 — Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders are open now.

What do you think?

title: Sketchy rumor again says OLED iPad mini will lack one key feature
snippet: Apple is widely expected to introduce a new OLED iPad mini as soon as later this month. A sketchy new rumor today once again claims the new iPad mini will switch to OLED but still have a 60Hz refresh rate and lack ProMotion support. more…
fullText:
Apple is widely expected to introduce a new OLED iPad mini as soon as later this month. A sketchy new rumor today once again claims the new iPad mini will switch to OLED but still have a 60Hz refresh rate and lack ProMotion support.

This is the second time we’ve heard this rumor, but both times it has come from the same source: the yeux1122 account on Naver. This account has a very mixed track record with Apple rumors. It often seems to regurgitate information from unnamed sources rather than provide its own.

Nonetheless, the latest post from yeux1122 claims “there is mention of 120Hz in some overseas sources” for the new OLED iPad mini, but “domestic production volume has already confirmed” it will use a 60Hz display.

Again, I’m treating this rumor with more than a healthy dose of skepticism, since no other reliable sources have corroborated it.

However, if it does come to fruition, this will be a disappointing limitation for iPad mini buyers. This iPad mini upgrade is expected to bring a number of other notable improvements, including:

An OLED display.

Apple’s A20 Pro chip, up from the current iPad mini’s A17 Pro chip.

A refreshed design with smaller bezels that could be more water-resistant.

The FaceTime camera will be relocated to the horizontal bezel, similar to Apple’s other iPad models.

	

If Apple made all those changes but stopped short of upgrading the display to ProMotion with a 120Hz refresh rate, it’d really sour the launch of the new iPad mini.

The new iPad mini is expected to launch later this month, so we don’t have much longer to wait to know for sure.

title: Fitbit Edge is Google’s middle ground between Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch
snippet: Google’s newest wearable costs $179.99 and has a sleek feel like the Fitbit Air but with an OLED display.
fullText:
Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch. 

Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls. 

Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule.

It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.)

Image Credits:Google

Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides, and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather.

The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips.

Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters.

The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27.

Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition, priced at $219.99.

title: The iPhone Duo’s cooling system hides a clever trick inside its hinge
snippet: While a folding iPhone posed a new challenge for Apple’s thermal engineering team, they came up with a creative way to leverage the device’s hinge to their advantage. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
While a folding iPhone posed a new challenge for Apple’s thermal engineering team, they came up with a creative way to leverage the device’s hinge to their advantage. Here are the details.

iPhone Duo’s hinge features a flexible graphite pipe

PCMag recently sat down with Dan Murray, Apple’s vice president of silicon engineering, and Banafsheh Barabadi, the company’s senior manager of thermal product design, to discuss the architecture of the A20 Pro chip.

The new SoC, which powers the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, is Apple’s first iPhone chip built on a 2 nm process, following the technology’s debut with the M6 chip in the Mac mini in August.

And while the A20 Pro was designed with all three new iPhones in mind, the iPhone Duo version packs some additional capabilities. These include a second display engine to run both screens simultaneously.

From PCMag:

The iPhone Duo’s A20 Pro variant is just slightly different. “For iPhone Duo, we added a second display engine to support simultaneous operation of the inner and outer displays,” says Murray, “and with the increased CPU and GPU performance, we ensure we can deliver a smooth user experience across the displays. For the inner display, we also added support for placing the FaceTime camera behind the display.”

The report offers a really interesting, in-depth look at the A20 Pro’s thermals and the new vapor chamber Apple developed to keep them at bay. That includes what Apple calls “metal over foam,” a material that iFixit also examined during its recent teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro.

The second pillar is a new material that bridges the gap between the A20 Pro and the vapor chamber. “We call it metal over foam,” says Barabadi, and it “basically creates a direct thermal and mechanically compliant coupling between the SoC and the vapor chamber. It is highly effective in removing the heat, meeting the strict mechanical requirements of the system. It took us months of development to get the material properties exactly right to be able to use this material.”

Perhaps the most interesting tidbit from the story is what Apple did to improve the iPhone Duo’s thermal performance, particularly given the challenges of dissipating heat in a device that doubles in thickness when folded.

From the report:

“This was one of the most technically challenging aspects of our design,” says Barabadi. To surmount the issue, Apple routed a flexible graphite pipe through the hinge itself to transfer heat between the two halves, thereby increasing the surface area available for heat dissipation. “This part need[ed] to be co-engineered between our thermal team and the mechanical team. It’s a flexible material that needs to survive, as you can imagine, many hinge cycles while maintaining its thermal connectivity, and also its structural integrity throughout the product life cycle.”

PCMag’s interview with Murray and Barabadi also goes into the A20 Pro’s architecture, including the benefits of placing the DRAM next to the processor rather than stacking it on top, and you can read it in full here.

The movie also stars Mark Ruffalo (Spotlight), Dylan O’Brien (Twinless), and Rob Delaney (Bad Monkey), among others, blending drama and humor to tell the true story of the 28-day occupation of the San Francisco Federal Building by disability rights protesters in 1977.

What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

“Being Heumann” is directed and produced by Siân Heder, whose 2021 film “CODA” earned Apple its first Best Picture Oscar in 2022. The film also won Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Supporting Actor for Troy Kotsur.

snippet: One of Apple TV’s hit comedy series from last year, Stick, is coming back for season 2 soon. Here’s the new trailer for Stick’s highly anticipated return. more…
fullText:
One of Apple TV’s hit comedy series from last year, Stick, is coming back for season 2 soon. Here’s the new trailer for Stick’s highly anticipated return.

Stick season 2 is coming November 4, here’s the trailer

Ted Lasso just wrapped up its fourth season, but Apple TV has another heartfelt sports comedy ready to take its place.

Stick returns for season 2 on Wednesday, November 4, with two episodes available initially then weekly releases through December 30.

Watch Stick on Apple TV

For the unfamiliar, Stick stars Owen Wilson as an ex-pro golfer—Pryce Cahill—whose career ended prematurely. But after helping train a 17-year-old golf phenom in season 1, the new season sees Cahill get back to the game himself.

And he’ll do it with the help of a new coach played by Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”).

Here’s Apple’s official season summary, followed by the new trailer:

In season two, Santi takes the next step in his pursuit of professional golf, only to discover how quickly the game changes when talent becomes expectation. As Santi chases his dream, Pryce finds himself wondering what might still be possible for him. Urged on by his former rival Clark Ross (Timothy Olyphant), Pryce does something nobody expects: he bets on himself, launching an improbable comeback in hopes of becoming the oldest golfer ever to win a major. But the road back proves far harder than he imagined. And the closer Pryce gets to the golfer he once was, the more he is forced to confront why he never fulfilled the promise everyone once saw in him. With brilliant new coach Amanda (Rhea Seehorn) and trusted caddie Mitts (Marc Maron) in his corner, Pryce sets out to prove — to the golf world and, more importantly, to himself — that maybe he really was as good as everyone always said he was.

In my experience, you don’t have to care about golf at all to enjoy Stick.

The show feels similar in spirit to other Apple comedies like Ted Lasso and Shrinking. In my view it especially hit its stride near the end of the season, so I’m excited to see it return.

title: Google announces $179 Fitbit Edge tracker with display, GPS
snippet: Google is following the Fitbit Air launched in May with a second tracker that features a screen called the Fitbit Edge. more…
fullText:
Google is following the Fitbit Air launched in May with a second tracker that features a screen called the Fitbit Edge.

The Fitbit Edge features a wide, pill-shaped AMOLED screen — protected by Gorilla Glass 3 — that offers 46% more display than the Charge 6 from 2023. The 11.5mm-thick body is made from precision-crafted aluminum with nano-molding technology to allow for a 40% more precise GPS (versus Charge 6), while there’s a dedicated altimeter for elevation tracking. On the right side, you’ll find a large button for tactile control, like when swimming. This device has IP68 / 5ATM dust and water protection.

On the underside, you’ll find the sensors. The Fitbit Edge has an accelerometer, altimeter, ambient light sensor, far-field skin temperature sensor, gyroscope, heart rate sensor, multipurpose electrical sensors (ECG), and red and infrared sensors (SpO2).

The Fitbit Edge uses the same magnetic USB-C charger as the Fitbit Air. A 5-minute charge gives you a day of battery, while a full top-up takes 90 minutes. Battery life is rated at a week with the always-on display disabled. When enabled, the Fitbit Edge comes in at around 2 days. Like the Pixel Watch 5, you can open the device to replace the battery.

	

The Fitbit Edge is available in the following colors:

Matte Black Aluminum case / Obsidian Active Band

Polished Silver Aluminum case / Fog Active Band

Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Olive Active Band

Champagne Gold case / Canyon Active Band

The bands are replaceable with a new swap mechanism and four additional designs: 

$39.99 Active Sport: Made of “ultra soft silicone” with large pill-shaped cutouts

$59.99 Magnet Band: Clasp-free design with magnets embedded into the strap

$149.99 Metal Links

$49.99 Performance Loop: Stretch and micro-adjustable

Supporting Android and iOS, the Edge is running a Fitbit operating system similar to the Air. A larger screen unlocks a richer interface that takes inspiration from the Pixel Watch 5.

Google showed a dozen or so watch faces for the Fitbit Edge with analog and digital options. You can customize what complications appear via the Google Health app.

Swiping left/right from the watch face lets you access various tiles, with the order customizable. This includes Quick start (for different exercises), Focus metrics, Sleep, Heart, Cycle health, Weather, Timers, Alarms, and Music controls.

Compared to the Charge 6, music controls work with any app on your paired device, while phone notifications are also available. Quick replies to messages are limited to Android due to iOS platform limitations. You also get Google Maps navigation, but there is no Google Wallet given the lack of NFC.

	

The Exercise app lets you track over 50 types of activity with real-time guidance and workout views. The Fitbit Edge can connect to equipment with heart rate broadcasting. 

The Fitbit Edge (and the Air) feature upgraded automatic activity detection. This AI-powered contextual reasoning can learn your habits over time to add support for over 100 activities. 

You can have the Fitbit Air, Edge, and Pixel Watch 5 operate on the same account with seamless switching.

The Fitbit Edge costs $179.99 with pre-orders open today and availability on October 27. A Stephen Curry Special Edition is available for $219.99 with a custom band.

title: iPhone Air 2 is coming, here’s everything we know so far
snippet: Apple is working on a second-generation iPhone Air, and it could address several key limitations of the current model. Here’s everything we know about the iPhone Air 2, including features, release date, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple is working on a second-generation iPhone Air, and it could address several key limitations of the current model. Here’s everything we know about the iPhone Air 2, including features, release date, and more.

Will there be an iPhone Air 2?

The iPhone Air has reportedly sold worse than Apple expected. The Information reported in November that Apple had indefinitely delayed the release of a second-generation model due to those lower-than-expected sales.

Apple reportedly “notified engineers and suppliers that they were taking the next iPhone Air off the schedule without providing a new release date.”

Shortly thereafter, however, The Information updated its reporting to say Apple wasn’t canceling the iPhone Air 2 altogether and that one is still very much in the works.

iPhone Air 2 features

A second camera

One of the biggest tradeoffs of the ultra-thin iPhone Air design is that it only has one camera. This is reportedly something Apple is pushing to change for the iPhone Air 2.

According to sources including Bloomberg and The Information, the iPhone Air 2 will have a second camera on the back.

Bloomberg says it will be an ultra-wide camera, not a telephoto camera. This would align it with Apple’s base model iPhones, which also have a main camera and an ultra-wide camera.

A20 Pro chip

The iPhone Air 2 will reportedly be powered by the A20 Pro processor, up from the A19 Pro in the current model.

The A20 Pro chip will be Apple’s first 2-nanometer iPhone processor. This new fabrication process will mean the A20 Pro can offer more power and be more efficient in a similar-sized footprint.

The chip will also use another new innovation called Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module, which integrates the SoC and DRAM at the wafer level for better performance and lower power consumption.

Better battery life

Apple is also reportedly working to improve the battery life of the iPhone Air 2.

According to a supply chain leak, the iPhone Air 2 will have a 3,500mAh battery. For comparison’s sake, the first-generation iPhone Air has a 3,149mAh battery, so this is an increase of more than 10%.

Beyond increasing the physical size of the battery, the iPhone Air 2 will likely offer longer battery life thanks to the efficiency improvements of the A20 Pro chip.

It’s important to remember, however, that there are many variables at play when it comes to an iPhone’s battery life. We’ll have to wait and see the exact numbers when Apple officially unveils the iPhone Air 2.

Vapor chamber

According to The Information, the iPhone Air 2 will feature a vapor chamber cooling system. Apple first debuted its vapor chamber cooling technology in the iPhone 17 Pro, touting significantly improved heat dissipation and performance.

If Apple brings the vapor chamber to the iPhone Air 2, it means the device will stay cooler during high workloads and sustain high performance for longer periods.

iPhone Air 2: Release date

The iPhone Air 2 was originally expected to be released in September 2026 alongside the iPhone 18 Pro lineup.

Most recently, however, Bloomberg reported that Apple plans to release the iPhone Air 2 in spring 2027 alongside the new base model iPhone 18.

title: Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 brings new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it packs key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it packs key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27.

Upgraded search

If you have much history using Apple Mail, you’ll know that its search feature hasn’t always been the best. But in iOS 27, search has gotten a big upgrade.

From Apple’s website:

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

I can’t count the number of times search has previously failed to find messages that I knew existed. So far in my testing, iOS 27 seems to have fixed that.

New suggestions that include third-party apps

Suggestions at the top of messages have been in Apple Mail for years. But in iOS 27, they get a new, more flexible design and expand to support third-party apps.

When Mail detects that you might want to take action on the contents of an email, a suggestion might appear at the top of the message. These include: directions in Maps, creating events in Calendar, tracking a shipment with Apple Wallet, and more.

In iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

Smart Reply improvements

Smart Reply is a keyboard feature that automatically surfaces reply options you can utilize with a single tap.

In iOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence comes with improvements to Smart Reply.

Apple says that Smart Reply “can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.” Essentially, rather than offering fairly generic reply options, now Smart Reply suggestions will actually sound a lot more like you.

Siri AI capabilities

Apple has added ‘Ask Siri’ buttons throughout Apple Mail, just like the rest of its system apps. And Siri AI brings a bunch of new powers for Mail users.

One example I’ve seen several times on social media already is that you can ask Siri to delete all messages from a specific sender that’s spamming you.

Bug fixes

Beyond new features, Apple also says that iOS 27 makes the Mail app run better than ever thanks to bug fixes and performance improvements. Here are some specific examples given:

Faster message loading in Mail

More reliable search indexing in Mail

Improved list formatting in Mail

Improved unread badge accuracy in Mail

title: Hands-on: Sonos Ace Ultra fix nearly everything I wanted from the original [Video]
snippet: I have been a huge Sonos fan and customer for years, dating back to the original Sonos One. So, about two years ago, when I heard that Sonos was entering the over-ear headphone market, I knew I had to give it a try. The Sonos Ace looked great, was very comfortable, and brought some cool Sonos ecosystem features. But for a premium pair of headphones, there were still a few areas that left me wanting more, like strong bass, better ANC, and a better app experience. fullText:
I have been a huge Sonos fan and customer for years, dating back to the original Sonos One. So, about two years ago, when I heard that Sonos was entering the over-ear headphone market, I knew I had to give it a try. The Sonos Ace looked great, was very comfortable, and brought some cool Sonos ecosystem features. But for a premium pair of headphones, there were still a few areas that left me wanting more, like strong bass, better ANC, and a better app experience. But now, the new Sonos Ace Ultra feels like they went down that list and addressed nearly every complaint that most customers had, including me. I have been using them as my main headphones for almost a month now, for travel, video editing, workouts, walks, and everyday listening. So I have a good grasp on them now, and here is what you need to know.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video review for the Sonos Ace Ultra below:

Sonos Ace Ultra

At first glance, the Sonos Ace Ultra does not look much different from the original Sonos Ace. They decided to keep the same clean, understated design with a few differently placed chrome accents and some additional colors. But the biggest differences are inside these headphones. 

What’s new versus the original Sonos Ace

Here are some of the biggest changes from the original Sonos Ace to the Ace Ultra:

Redesigned 40mm drivers

10-microphone array, up from eight mics on the original

Improved adaptive ANC, stating up to 2X more effective and being able to adjust to things like glasses, hair, and changes in the seal around your ears

Longer battery life with up to 35 hours with ANC turned on

Bluetooth 6.0 versus 5.4 on the older generation

Expanded EQ controls with three and an advanced eight-band EQ options

Headphones linking with the Sonos Ecosystem

User-replaceable batteries

Updated ear and headband cushion materials  

More rotation of the ear cups so they can sit flat when around your neck

Two new colors: Agave and Sand

The main things that I noticed in these changes are the redesigned acoustics, better bass response, and stronger ANC. With the original Sonos Ace, I would sometimes get this hissing noise when I was in ANC mode. This would rarely happen, but I did notice it. So far, the new Sonos Ace Ultra has alleviated that issue. You also still get some of the great specs from the previous model like:

Spatial audio and Dolby Atmos

Dynamic head tracking

Lossless audio on supported devices

USB-C and 3.5mm wired audio support

Bluetooth multipoint

Fast charging with up to three hours of playback from a three-minute charge

TV Audio Swap with compatible Sonos soundbars

They still have the same super high-quality design, combining plastics and metals to give you a premium, lightweight feel. The Sonos Ace Ultra also keeps the magnetically replaceable ear cups, and one of the best things that I have noticed is the new EQ settings that really let me hone in on how I like to listen to my music. But how were they as an everyday pair of headphones?

My experience

Again, it’s easy to put specs on paper, but the biggest reason I’ve enjoyed the Ace Ultras is that they actually sound noticeably better. My biggest complaint about the original Sonos Ace was the lack of bass depth. The bass was not bad, but for a pair of $450 headphones, I felt like they were lacking a bit. I listen to a lot of R&B, hip-hop, and pop music, so bass is important to me. I wanted more low-end impact and to feel the bass. The Ace Ultra finally delivers the experience that I wanted. 

There is substantially more punch and depth at the low end. But one thing to note here is that Sonos hasn’t achieved that by simply turning up the bass slider. Any headphone brand can crank up the bass, but the difficult part is maintaining separation so that the bass doesn’t overwhelm the vocals, instruments, and higher-end frequencies. That is where the Ace Ultra has really impressed me. The bass hits harder, but the vocals are still clear, crisp, and easy to listen to. And it’s not just for music; all media sounds better, like podcasts, movies, and all the YouTube videos I watch. They have sounded fantastic in all media listening situations. 

The improved ANC is something else I noticed immediately. The new 10 mic array allows even more sound to be dynamically pushed away from the headphones. Even when there is no media playing, it’s insane how quiet the headphones are in so many different environments. It’s almost too good! The biggest improvement to ANC is the unpredictable noises. It’s one thing to block out a consistent noise like an airplane engine, but another to block out passing cars, construction, sirens, or sudden loud sounds while walking outside.

Two final things I want to bring up are comfort and the Sonos ecosystem. These headphones are the most comfortable headphones I have worn. Even on a long 8-10-hour airplane ride, I wore them 95% of the time, and I felt no aches, pain, or heat at all. Lastly, I have a lot of Sonos speakers around my house, and they introduced a new feature that lets you move music from a speaker to your headphones with the press of a button. It’s a very cool feature, but I personally haven’t used it much.

My only complaint is that they need a new zipper or mechanism for the headphone case because that sticker gets stuck way too often!

Pricing and availability 

The Sonos Ace Ultra is available today on Sonos’s site and Amazon for $449, keeping the same launch price as the original Sonos Ace. They come in four colors: Black, White, Agave, and Sand. I also noticed that the original Sonos Ace is available on Amazon for $239 while supplies last. At $240, now that could be a good choice as well.

At $450, the Sonos Ace Ultra is firmly in the premium noise-canceling headphone category alongside options from Apple, Bose, and Sony.

Final take

The original Sonos Ace felt like a good first-generation product. The Sonos Ace Ultra feels like a complete and finished product. As we saw, they did not reinvent the look or design, but they improved in all the areas that mattered and even added a few new cool features. The sound is noticeably better, the ANC is strong and smarter, battery life lasts longer, the app experience is smoother, and that Agave color is amazing.

If you already own the OG Sonos Ace, I actually think there is enough here to justify the upgrade, depending on what you value. If you are in the market for a premium set of headphones, I think the Sonos Ace Ultra needs to be on your shortlist. At $449, they are certainly not cheap, but if you want one of the best premium headphones and are a Sonos fan, then you will love these.

title: Grok Bot just got its own email address, here’s how to claim yours
snippet: Grok Bot just got a second significant upgrade this week: its own email address. more…
fullText:
Grok Bot just got a second significant upgrade this week: its own email address. 

“Bot can use it to sign up for services, contact businesses for you, or schedule time with someone,” per the announcement on X.

“Rolling out to users today. To claim your inbox, just ask Bot or tag @bot on X,” the announcement explains.

title: MagSafe Monday: This aluminum MagSafe wallet ejects your credit card with one click
snippet: My biggest annoyance with all types of wallets is when it This aluminum MagSafe card wallet takes a different approach with a side-mounted eject button that fans your cards up with a single press, so you can grab the one you need one-handed without pulling them all out. more…
fullText:
My biggest annoyance with all types of wallets is when it This aluminum MagSafe card wallet takes a different approach with a side-mounted eject button that fans your cards up with a single press, so you can grab the one you need one-handed without pulling them all out. 

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

The eject button is the best part

Hands down, the best part of this wallet is the eject button. The side button slides to fan your cards upward so you can grab whichever one you need without removing the wallet from your iPhone. This is the reason to buy this wallet over others as its the main unique thing. If you’re the type who keeps one card in a wallet and never needs to choose between them, a basic slot MagSafe wallet is probably fine. If you’re carrying two or three cards and want to pick the right one quickly at checkout, the ejector earns its keep.

The wallet is machined from lightweight aluminum with a scratch-resistant finish, and it comes in a bunch of different colors if you want it to match your iPhone or case. The wallet uses 32 built-in magnetic strips to snap onto a MagSafe compatible iPhone. I haven’t used it long enough to know how the finish holds up, but it feels solid.

The aluminum housing claims it blocks 13.56MHz RFID frequencies, so your contactless credit cards and ID are protected from electronic skimming in airports, etc. This is worth knowing upfront: this wallet holds up to 3 cards. That covers most everyday carry setups, but if you’re someone who needs four or five cards accessible, this isn’t the right fit. Three cards, one eject button, and a metal build is the whole point here. If this held 5 cards, it would honestly be perfect.

I wish it had Find My support, but it doesnt. If Find My matter to you, you’ll need to look elsewhere, but if you want a clean metal MagSafe wallet with a fast card ejector and solid MagSafe hold, this does this job well.

Wrap up

The eject button is what makes this MagSafe wallet worth buying. This one has a mechanism that actually speeds up the process of getting a card. The RDID blocking functionality is also pretty nice as well. The Metal housing is not something I’ve used in a wallet before, so it’s been a change, but overall I like it. Again, the downside is that it’s limited to 3 cards only.

You can buy it from Amazon.

title: Apple refreshes its HomePod mini with a new chip and $149 price tag
snippet: The new $149 HomePod mini with Siri AI and a 'SoundGlow' visual feature will be available starting October 30.
fullText:
Image Credits:Apple	

	

						

6:38 AM PDT · October 13, 2026

											

			

Apple’s new HomeView device was the center of the show at its smart home event on Tuesday, but the company also refreshed its HomePod mini smart speaker with a new chip and Siri AI integration, the latter of which will be available through a future update.

The $149 update is $50 more expensive than the original version launched over six years ago in 2020. The new HomePod mini has an S10 chip that helps improve optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance.

With the new HomePod mini, users can control their smart home devices through voice commands. Plus, the speaker can listen for sounds like a smoke alarm and send a notification to users’ phones — a feature that Alexa devices have offered for years.

Apple said that with Siri AI, users will be able to have multi-turn conversations, but it didn’t provide a date for when the new assistant will be available to HomePod mini 2 buyers.

The company also said the new speaker works better with its other devices. For instance, users could form a four-speaker home entertainment system paired with the new Apple TV 4K. Plus, the HomePod mini 2 speakers can be the default speaker for Mac for video calls or music playback instead of built-in speakers.

The device has another new feature, as well: a visual canvas called “Sound Glow,” which uses the color scheme of the album art to turn the top of the HomePod mini into a visual canvas that will glow and pulse in sync with the music. Users can also pick soundscapes like rain or ocean waves to start animations.

The new speaker comes in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight colorways and will be available starting October 30. Consumers can preorder starting today.

title: These US states just said ‘no’ to Apple Wallet driver’s licenses
snippet: Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all. more…
fullText:
Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all.

Florida and Rhode Island won’t be getting Apple Wallet driver’s licenses anytime soon, per key leaders

The number of US states offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps growing, and we even have a good idea of three states launching support soon.

Plenty of states likely intend to support digital driver’s licenses at some point, and haven’t gotten around to it. But there are two who recently indicated they have no plans to launch support.

Those two states are:

Florida

Rhode Island

Last week, Florida rolled out a brand new driver’s license and ID card. Many states take such occasions to launch digital versions too, but the state made zero announcements around digital ID.

That’s no coincidence, as Governor Ron DeSantis actively opposes the idea of digital driver’s licenses. He posted the following on X last November:

The convenience of a digital drivers license is outweighed by the potential for government to abuse it.  

Not gonna happen in FL.  

No digital ID. https://t.co/YD7J6PtBgR

— Ron DeSantis (@RonDeSantis) November 28, 2025

Florida previously did offer a digital ID but abruptly ended support in 2024. Perhaps the next governor will take a different stance.

In Rhode Island, Walter “Bud” Craddock was on a podcast last week discussing mobile driver’s licenses (“MDL”). Craddock is currently Chair of the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators (AAMVA) International Board of Directors.

	

Here’s what he said:

“I want to see more universal adoption or need for an MDL. I had one of my senators approach and try to talk me into doing it. I had to give him the old Heisman move and push him back…the main user right now is TSA. Up until recently, there was no airport in New England area that could accept an MDL. So why would I spend the money in the development of it? And also, I’m looking to do a solution that is across all platforms. Instead of just doing one for Apple or the Google Wallets, I don’t want to replicate and duplicate efforts.”

Like DeSantis, Craddock’s position of leadership is slated to end in the next few months. So depending on his successor’s stance, perhaps Rhode Island could get Apple Wallet driver’s licenses sometime in 2027.

Here’s the full list of US states currently offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses, and three expected to launch next.

title: Review: Rhinoshield’s iPhone 18 Pro bumper case is minimalist but surprisingly protective
snippet: iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case. more…
fullText:
iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case.

Apple finally got back into the bumper business with the iPhone Air last year. I was hoping Apple would expand their bumper case to the iPhone 18 Pro (like they did with the clear case and iPhone 11), but unfortunately they did not. In my search for another option, I came across Rhinoshield’s Minimalist Impact Bumper case. 

Key Details

The Impact Bumper Case has a fit similar to most other bumpers, where the lip on the screen is fairly minor, while the lip on the back is a little larger. A unique feature of this case, and one that I quite like, is that it has special supports that keep the camera plateau and lenses off of wherever your phone is resting, which I particularly appreciate considering the aluminum 17 Pro and 18 Pro. This results in a far more protective case than your typical bumper would be. It also eliminates the annoying wobble when using your phone on a flat surface.

The case’s fit, however, is not quite what I was hoping for. It’s somewhat loose, and you can easily bend the edges outward, and I do wonder if over time they may end up getting stretched out. I don’t think the phone flying out of the case when dropped will be an issue though (and I have unintentionally tested that). That said, the material of the entire case is a hard plastic rather than rubber, so hopefully it will be fine in the long run. Rhinoshield says that it is made entirely of just one material, and is therefore 100% recyclable.

The case comes in three colors, which are matched to the iPhone 18 Pro colors: white, blue, and black (sorry Burgundy fans). The blue, which is what I have, is close to Glacier but not perfect. 

Downsides

There are some downsides, however. My primary gripe with the case is that the buttons can be hard to press. For some reason they went with a nearly flush design, and the way that the buttons are designed makes them mushy. 

The material choice as a whole may be a downside. To me, it feels cheaper than the likes of Apple’s iPhone Air bumper, but some may end up preferring it. I certainly prefer it to the materials of a typical TPU/rubber clear case. The material and loose design also seem to attract pocket dust.

If you use Apple’s Wrist Strap or Crossbody Strap, be aware that this case does not have the required loop connection points. 

Conclusion

The Rhinoshield bumper is definitely not perfect, and I still hope that Apple will extend their bumpers to other iPhones. In the end though, I have decided to keep the case, for one primary reason: it lets me have a near-caseless experience without worry of the fragile aluminum getting chipped or dented. As far as I can tell, the bumper case is usually only available from their own website, so the price of about $30 matches the price of Apple’s ($39) after shipping. You can get the Rhinoshield Minimalist Impact Bumper case here. (Occasionally, an Amazon listing will pop up, so you can give that a try as well.)

title: Pixel 11 series still not on Android 17 QPR1 with October update
snippet: With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1. more…
fullText:
With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1.

The Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold launched in August with the base Android 17 release. In September, the Pixel 11 series received two early updates that presumably addressed issues that emerged since launch. 

	

Later in the month, Google rolled out QPR1 to all other devices. Visual changes in the quarterly release include system blur for the volume slider and power menu, while there’s an updated system media player that gets narrower when other apps are available. The Mobile Data Quick Settings Tile gets a time-saving “Don’t ask me again” toggle, while there’s now a Keyboard QS Tile.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 series did not get the initial Android 17 QPR2 Beta 6 release and had to wait a few days for Beta 6.1, which introduced HiLight support for message notifications. It did get the 17 QPR3 Beta without issue a few days later. 

	

This week’s October release does contain fixes for the Pixel 11:

Fix for issue causing the virtual keyboard to occasionally not appear when interacting with search input fields*[1]

Fix for issue occasionally causing captured photos or recorded videos to save in the incorrect orientation*[3]

It’s unlikely that we’ll get a second October release, with all eyes on November. With QPR2 just a month away at that point, Google might wait for December to align all the devices.

title: Google rolling out ‘massive’ Pixel Buds Pro 2 and 2a update [U]
snippet: Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update. more…
fullText:
Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update.

Update 10/7: Google has reached out to clarify that these updates are only for the Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a. The original Pixel Buds Pro, which has since been removed from the announcement, are not getting these new features.

The only feature exclusive to the Pixel Buds Pro 2 is Dynamic Active Noise Cancellation. Google will “automatically adjust audio or noise cancellation based on your ear seal.” This compensates for “subtle shifts” when the buds move in your ear.

The remaining features are available for the Pixel Buds Pro 2 (2024) and 2a (2025). When these features were previewed in August, Google did not mention that the original Pro model would be getting this update.

	

With last month’s Pixel Buds companion app update, you can turn on Active Noise Cancellation, adjust EQ, and enable touch controls with Gemini voice commands.

	

During phone calls, Tap to Mute lets you mute and unmute the microphone by tapping the buds. This gesture requires a paired Pixel phone.

Pixel Buds can now auto-pause media playback when you fall asleep, which is determined by Pixel Watch sleep sensing. This will also disable touch gestures and silence notifications.

The final update is Enhanced Live Translate that allows you to “leave your phone in your pocket and start translating instantly with a simple touch on your earbuds.”

Whether you’re conversing with someone or using listening mode to stay aware of your surroundings in a foreign language, Pixel Buds work seamlessly with the Google Translate app to make on-the-go translation easier than ever.

Make sure you’re running the latest version of the Pixel Buds app, and be on the lookout for software release_6.144. Open the companion client and scroll down for More settings > Firmware update to check.

title: Apple, Prosser, and Ramacciotti trade blame over delays in trade secret lawsuit
snippet: In a joint status report made public earlier today, Apple said it is still waiting on additional documents from Jon Prosser and wants to depose Michael Ramacciotti again, while both defendants pushed back on the company’s handling of the case. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a joint status report made public earlier today, Apple said it is still waiting on additional documents from Jon Prosser and wants to depose Michael Ramacciotti again, while both defendants pushed back on the company’s handling of the case. Here are the details.

According to a joint status report to Judge James Donato, Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti are increasingly at odds over who is responsible for delays in the trade secret lawsuit Apple filed against both defendants in July 2025.

A bit of context

As a refresher, soon after announcing iOS 26, Apple filed a trade secret misappropriation lawsuit against Prosser and Ramacciotti over Prosser’s videos, where he leaked aspects of the system, including what turned out to be the Liquid Glass visual revamp.

Apple said Ramacciotti improperly accessed the development iPhone of an employee, who was later fired over the incident, and held a FaceTime call with Prosser to show him unreleased iOS features running on the device.

Since then, the case has had its own share of drama, with the clerk’s entry of default after Prosser failed to respond to Apple’s complaint by the deadline (although Prosser has disputed the characterization that he had ignored the case).

Then, eight months later, the court agreed to set that default aside and give him another chance to formally contest the allegations.

Court documents show that Ramacciotti, on the other hand, responded to Apple’s complaint and has largely cooperated with the company’s discovery requests.

Since Prosser retained representation and formally entered the case, however, things have taken a turn, with all three sides increasingly disagreeing over who is responsible for the alleged trade secret disclosure and for the delays that have followed.

The new joint status report

Back to the new status report, Apple says it wants Ramacciotti to update his interrogatory responses and sit for another deposition to address what it describes as “inconsistencies between his and Mr. Prosser’s testimony.”

Ramacciotti, however, says he will sit for another deposition once Apple provides “a roadmap to resolution of its claims against him, including what more, if anything, Apple needs from him.”

When it comes to Prosser, Apple says it “continues to await his production of certain additional documents that it requested over three months ago. These include revenue reports and data analytics for his YouTube channels and relevant communications with third parties that he identified during his deposition.”

Prosser, in turn, argues that “[i]t appears that the Trade Secrets at issue are no longer trade secrets and are in the public domain.” In other words, his argument appears to be that since Apple released the iOS update with Liquid Glass, the information at the center of the lawsuit is now publicly available and therefore no longer qualifies as secret.

As part of the joint status update, Ramacciotti asks the court to hold a status conference this month, at which Apple would be required to explain what additional information it still needs from him. He also wants Apple to then have 30 days to either dismiss its claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial.

Apple, meanwhile, wants discovery to continue, including a second deposition of Ramacciotti and the outstanding documents from Prosser. Prosser argues that he has already complied with the discovery obligations he agreed to and pushes back on Apple’s continuing requests for additional material.

If Judge Donato does not grant Ramacciotti’s request for a status conference, the parties propose filing another joint status report on December 2.
